title: Stretching and springs: things that bounce back

summary.text: This unit is about stretching and springing back. Some things, like a rubber band or a spring, change shape when you pull or squash them. Then they go back to their old shape when you let go. Scientists call this being elastic. The harder you pull a spring, the further it stretches. But stretch anything too far and it stays stretched, or it snaps. A stretched or squashed thing also stores energy, ready to fling a stone, wind a watch or bounce a ball. Deep down, things spring back because their atoms are held together by tiny electric pulls that act like springs. The same idea reaches out to your own tendons and to earthquakes. It even reaches space itself, which stretches and squeezes as gravitational waves pass.
summary.art: A child pulling a rubber band between two fingers; behind, faint pictures of a jumping flea, a mango branch bending under a swing, and the Earth with ripples of stretched space around it.

intro.hook: Take a rubber band. Stretch it a little and let go. Now take a strip of plastic from an old carry bag. Stretch that a little and let go. One of them came back. One of them did not. Why?
intro.text: In Kerala, rubber begins as a white milk that drips from the bark of rubber trees. Farmers dry it into sheets. Before selling a sheet, they pull one corner. A good sheet stretches and slides back flat. A sheet that stretches and stays stretched is old and close to tearing. Why does a thing that stops coming back matter so much? This unit is about stretching and coming back. Scientists call it being elastic.
intro.art: A hand pulling the corner of a brown rubber sheet, which stretches and then slides back flat, with rows of rubber trees behind.

outcomes: I can say what elastic means: a thing changes shape when pushed or pulled, and goes back when you let go. I can name elastic things at home.
I can run a fair test of how far a rubber band stretches as I add weight, and show my results in a table and a line graph.
I can explain the elastic limit: stretch too far and a thing stays stretched or snaps. I can sort things into elastic, stays-changed and snaps.
I can explain that a stretched or squashed spring stores energy, and give uses like catapults, wind-up toys, bows and bouncing balls.
I can find springs and elastic parts in machines, in nature and in my own body, and say what job each one does.
I can explain, deep down, why things spring back: atoms held by tiny electric pulls that act like springs, and rubber's tangled chains.
I can give big examples of stretching: earthquakes, the Earth ringing like a bell, and space itself stretching as gravitational waves pass. I can say what scientists still do not know.

terms.meaning: A push or a pull. Forces can make things move, stop, turn or change shape.
terms.example: You pull a rubber band. You squash a sponge. Both are forces.
terms.art: Two hands: one pulling a rubber band, one squashing a sponge.

terms.meaning: To pull something so it gets longer.
terms.example: You stretch a rubber band round a bundle of pencils.
terms.art: A rubber band before and after stretching, with a ruler beside it.

terms.meaning: To push on something so it gets shorter or flatter. Scientists also say compress.
terms.example: Pressing the top of a clicky pen squashes the spring inside.
terms.art: A spring being squashed flat by a thumb.

terms.meaning: A thing is elastic if it changes shape when pushed or pulled, and goes back to its old shape when you let go.
terms.example: A rubber band, a spring, a sponge and a bouncy ball are all elastic.
terms.art: Four things in a row, each shown squashed or stretched, then back to normal.

terms.meaning: A coil of springy metal wire. Pull it and it gets longer. Squash it and it gets shorter. Let go and it goes back.
terms.example: There is a small spring inside a clicky ballpoint pen.
terms.art: A clicky pen opened up, with its little spring lying beside it.

terms.meaning: To go back to the old shape after being stretched, squashed or bent.
terms.example: Press a sponge. Let go. It springs back.
terms.art: A sponge, pressed and then puffed back up.

terms.meaning: A thing that changes shape and stays changed when you let go. Scientists call this plastic, which is a different meaning from plastic bags.
terms.example: Playdough, chewing gum and a strip from a thin carry bag stay stretched.
terms.art: A ball of playdough pulled long, staying long after the hands let go.

terms.meaning: A thing that hardly bends at all, then suddenly breaks. Scientists call this brittle.
terms.example: A dry twig, a papad and a glass bangle snap.
terms.art: A dry twig snapping in two, with a little crack line.

terms.meaning: The furthest you can stretch a thing and still have it spring back. Go past it and the thing stays stretched or breaks.
terms.example: Pull a pen spring very hard. It stays long and wobbly. It went past its elastic limit.
terms.art: Two pen springs: one neat, one pulled long and loose.

terms.meaning: The force a stretched or squashed thing makes as it tries to go back to its old shape. Scientists call it the restoring force.
terms.example: A stretched rubber band pulls back on your fingers.
terms.art: Two fingers holding a stretched band, with small arrows pointing inwards.

terms.meaning: Hard to stretch or bend. A stiff spring needs a big pull to stretch a little.
terms.example: A cycle seat spring is much stiffer than a pen spring.
terms.art: A thick cycle seat spring next to a thin pen spring.

terms.meaning: Energy waiting inside something, ready to be used. A stretched or squashed spring stores energy.
terms.example: When you let go of a stretched catapult, the stored energy flings the paper ball.
terms.art: A popsicle-stick catapult, bent back, with a glowing 'stored energy' halo.

terms.meaning: When a thing hits the ground, squashes a little, then springs back and jumps up.
terms.example: A rubber ball bounces high. A ball of clay just goes splat.
terms.art: A rubber ball squashed flat for a moment on the floor, then rising.

terms.meaning: A graph where dots are joined by a line. It shows how one thing changes as another thing changes.
terms.example: A line graph can show how long a rubber band gets as you add more coins.
terms.art: A simple line graph going up in a straight line.

terms.meaning: The tiny building block that everything is made of. Atoms are far too small to see, even with an ordinary microscope.
terms.example: Your rubber band is made of countless atoms, all holding on to each other.
terms.art: A zoom from a rubber band to a tangle of chains to tiny balls.

terms.meaning: The pull that holds two atoms together. A bond acts a bit like a tiny spring between them.
terms.example: In a steel spring, atoms are joined by bonds. Stretching the spring stretches the bonds a tiny bit.
terms.art: Balls joined by small springs, like a ball-and-spring toy.

terms.meaning: A very long chain made of many small bits joined in a row. Rubber is made of polymers.
terms.example: Rubber is made of long, tangled chains, like a bowl of cooked noodles.
terms.art: A bowl of tangled noodles next to a drawing of tangled rubber chains.

terms.meaning: A strong, stretchy cord that joins a muscle to a bone. Tendons work like springs when you run and jump.
terms.example: The thick cord at the back of your ankle is your Achilles tendon.
terms.art: A child's leg with the Achilles tendon glowing at the back of the ankle.

terms.meaning: A sudden shaking of the ground. It happens when rocks that were slowly bent underground suddenly slip and spring back.
terms.example: The ground shakes, and the lights swing.
terms.art: Two blocks of rock bent like a ruler, then slipping with a jolt.

terms.meaning: A ripple in space itself. As it passes, it stretches space one way and squeezes it the other way, by an incredibly tiny amount.
terms.example: In 2015, scientists first caught a gravitational wave from two black holes that crashed together.
terms.art: A grid of space rippling out from two black holes spiralling together.

terms.meaning: To shake back and forth very fast. A plucked rubber band vibrates because it keeps springing back past its middle.
terms.example: Pluck a stretched rubber band. It blurs and hums.
terms.art: A plucked rubber band with blur lines and a little musical note.

explanations.definition: A thing is elastic if it changes shape when a force pushes or pulls it, and goes back to its old shape when the force stops.
explanations.description: Pull a rubber band and it gets longer. Let go and it snaps back. Squeeze a sponge and it gets smaller. Let go and it puffs back up. Both are elastic. Being elastic is not only about stretching. Things can also be squashed, bent or twisted and then spring back. Here is a surprise. Steel, wood, stone and even glass are a little elastic too. They just need a much bigger force before you can see them change.
examples: A hair band stretches round your hair, then goes back to its small loop.
A plastic ruler bends when you press its end, then springs straight.
A cricket ball squashes a tiny bit when the bat hits it, then springs back round.
explanations.art: Four panels: a rubber band stretched and back, a sponge squeezed and back, a ruler bent and back, a ball squashed and back.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what it means for something to be elastic.

explanations.concept: Springs: stretch springs and squash springs
explanations.definition: A spring is a coil of springy metal wire. Some springs are made to be stretched, and some are made to be squashed. Both push or pull back when you let go.
explanations.description: A stretch spring has its coils packed tightly together. You pull its ends apart. A squash spring has gaps between its coils. You press its ends together. The spring in a clicky pen is a squash spring. The spring inside a spring balance at the vegetable shop is a stretch spring. Making the wire into a coil lets a short piece of stiff steel stretch a long way. Each bit of the wire twists only a little, but all the little twists add up.
examples: A clicky pen has a squash spring. It pushes the tip back in.
A trampoline has stretch springs all round its edge.
A clothes peg has a twisty spring that snaps its jaws shut.
explanations.art: Two springs side by side: a stretch spring with tight coils being pulled, and a squash spring with gaps being pressed.
explanations.context: Springs are hiding in pens, beds and cycles. This card explains the two main kinds.

explanations.definition: The harder you pull a spring, the longer it stretches. Double the pull and you get about double the stretch. This works until you get near the spring's limit.
explanations.description: Hang a cup from a rubber band and add coins, 5 at a time. Each time, measure the band. For many springs, each 5 coins add the same extra length. Joined up on a line graph, the dots make a straight line. Robert Hooke, an English scientist, wrote this rule down in 1678. He put it in Latin: 'as the stretch, so the force'. It is now called Hooke's law. Steel springs follow it closely. Rubber bands follow it only roughly. This rule is why a forcemeter, a tool that measures pulls, has evenly spaced marks. The unit on measuring forces looks at forcemeters more closely.
examples: One bag of shopping stretches the spring of a luggage scale a little. Two bags stretch it about twice as far.
A thick rubber band needs a bigger pull than a thin one to stretch the same amount. Scientists say it is stiffer.
explanations.art: A rubber band hanging from a pencil with a paper cup below it, coins going in, and a ruler beside it.
explanations.context: Have you noticed a heavier bag stretches a rubber band more? This card explains the rule behind it, with made-up results from the coin test.

chart.title: Made-up example: length of a rubber band as coins are added
chart.note: Each 5 coins made the band about 1 cm longer. The line is straight.

explanations.concept: The elastic limit: spring back, stay stretched, or snap
explanations.definition: Every elastic thing has a limit. Stretch it less than its limit and it springs back. Stretch it past its limit and it stays stretched, or it snaps.
explanations.description: Pull a pen spring gently and it springs back neat. Pull it hard and it stays long and loose. It has gone past its elastic limit. Scientists sort materials into three kinds. Elastic things spring back, like rubber. Stay-changed things, like playdough and chewing gum, keep their new shape. Scientists call this plastic. Snapping things, like a dry twig or a papad, hardly bend before they break. Scientists call this brittle. Many things do all three. A steel spoon springs back from a small bend. Push hard and it stays bent. Bend it back and forth many times and it can snap.
examples: A rubber band left round a newspaper for months goes loose and floppy.
A green twig bends and springs back. A dry twig snaps.
A strip cut from a thin carry bag stretches long and stays long.
explanations.art: Three hands: one pulling a rubber band that springs back, one pulling playdough that stays long, one bending a dry twig that snaps.
explanations.context: Can you stretch something for ever? This card explains what happens when you stretch too far.

explanations.definition: When you stretch, squash, bend or twist an elastic thing, the work you do is stored inside it. Let go, and the stored energy can make something move.
explanations.description: Energy is what it takes to make something move, warm up or change. When you pull back a catapult, your arm puts energy into the stretched rubber. When you let go, the rubber springs back and gives that energy to the stone or paper ball. The more you stretch, the more energy is stored, until the elastic limit. People have used stored elastic energy for thousands of years. Bows fling arrows. Wind-up watches and toys run on a tightly coiled spring. Some old mechanical clocks run for a whole week on one winding.
examples: A wind-up toy car runs when its twisted spring unwinds.
A bow made of bamboo bends back, stores energy, and flings the arrow.
A twisted rubber band can turn the propeller of a toy plane.
explanations.art: A child pulling back a bamboo bow, with a glowing band showing energy stored in the bent bow.
explanations.context: Why does a stretched catapult fling a paper ball? This card explains that stretching stores energy.

explanations.concept: Bouncing is a squash and a spring back
explanations.definition: When a ball hits the floor, it squashes for a very short moment. Then it springs back and pushes itself up. That is a bounce.
explanations.description: The squash is too quick to see. Slow-motion films show a tennis ball going flat on one side when it lands. Wet a ball and drop it on a dry floor, and the wet mark shows how big the squashed part was. No ball bounces all the way back up. Some of the energy turns into heat and sound each time. A rubber ball keeps more of its energy, so it bounces higher. A ball of clay is not elastic. It squashes and stays squashed, so it does not bounce at all. Tennis has a rule about bounce. A tennis ball dropped from 254 cm must bounce back up between 135 cm and 147 cm.
examples: A bouncy rubber ball bounces higher than a sponge ball.
A trampoline's springs and stretchy mat squash down under you, then push you up.
explanations.art: A slow-motion strip: a ball falling, squashing flat on the floor, then springing back up a little lower than it started.
explanations.context: Why do some balls bounce high and others don't bounce at all? This card explains what a bounce really is.

explanations.concept: Deep down: atoms held by tiny springs
explanations.definition: Solid things are elastic because their atoms are held together by electric pulls called bonds. A bond acts like a tiny spring between two atoms.
explanations.description: Zoom far into a steel spring. You find atoms in neat rows. Each atom is pulled towards its neighbours by electric forces. Push atoms closer and they push apart. Pull them further apart and they pull together. So every bond is like a tiny spring. When you stretch a steel spring, you stretch countless bonds a tiny bit each. Let go, and the bonds pull the atoms back to their places. Past the elastic limit, rows of atoms slide over each other into new places. They do not slide back. That is why a stretched-too-far spring stays long. Atoms on their bonds are never perfectly still. They jiggle all the time, even at the coldest temperature possible.
examples: Scientists often build models of solids with little balls joined by springs.
Heat makes atoms jiggle more on their bonds. That is why a metal rod gets very slightly longer when it is hot.
explanations.art: A zoom in four steps: a steel spring; the wire; rows of atoms; atoms joined by tiny springs, stretched a little.
explanations.context: This card zooms in far past anything a microscope can show. It finds out why things spring back, deep down.

explanations.definition: Rubber is made of very long, tangled chains of atoms called polymers. Stretching straightens the chains. They spring back because jiggling atoms shake them back into a tangle.
explanations.description: Think of a bowl of cooked noodles, all tangled. Pull them and they line up straight. In rubber, the chains are joined to each other here and there, so they cannot slide apart. When you let go, the chains are shaken by the jiggling of heat. Tangled is far more likely than straight, so they wriggle back into a tangle. This is why rubber does odd things. It warms up when you stretch it fast. It cools when it springs back. A stretched rubber band even pulls harder when you heat it. John Gough, a blind scientist in England, found the warming in 1805. He held rubber against his lips while he stretched it. Much later, in 1859, James Joule measured it carefully.
examples: Stretch a thick rubber band quickly and hold it to your forehead. It feels warm.
Cold rubber goes stiff, because its chains jiggle less.
explanations.art: A bowl of tangled noodles, then the same noodles pulled straight, then rubber chains tangled and straightened beside them.
explanations.context: A steel spring and a rubber band both spring back, but for different reasons. This card explains rubber's secret.

explanations.definition: Living bodies are full of elastic parts. Tendons, skin, lungs and blood vessels stretch and spring back. Some animals store energy in springs to jump.
explanations.description: When you run, the tendon at the back of your ankle stretches as you land. It springs back as you push off, and gives back much of the energy. The arch of your foot works as a spring too. Kangaroos hop a long way using huge springy tendons in their legs. A flea jumps using a pad of a rubbery stuff called resilin. Torkel Weis-Fogh, a Danish scientist, discovered resilin in insect wings in 1960. The flea squashes the pad, locks it, then lets go all at once. Your skin springs back when pinched, because of a stretchy stuff called elastin. Your biggest blood vessel stretches with each heartbeat and springs back, which keeps blood flowing smoothly. Inside your muscles is titin, the biggest protein your body makes. It works like a tiny spring.
examples: Pinch the skin on the back of your hand and let go. It springs back.
A spider's web stretches when an insect hits it, instead of breaking.
The mantis shrimp, a sea animal, punches with a spring in its arm. Sheila Patek and her team filmed it in 2004.
explanations.art: A child mid-jump with the Achilles tendon glowing; around them a kangaroo, a flea, a spider web and a mantis shrimp.
explanations.context: Your body is full of springs. This card looks at the elastic parts of living things, from tendons to flea legs.

explanations.concept: Bend, don't break: why springy things survive
explanations.definition: A thing that can bend and spring back can take a sudden heavy push without breaking. A stiff, brittle thing may snap instead.
explanations.description: When a heavy load suddenly lands on something, its energy has to go somewhere. A springy thing bends, stores the energy for a moment, then gives it back. A stiff, brittle thing cannot bend, so the force builds up until it cracks. That is why bamboo bends in a storm instead of snapping. A green mango branch bends under a swing and springs back. Bent past its limit, it stays bent, and that is the warning that it may break. Tall buildings are designed to sway a little in strong winds, for the same reason.
examples: A coconut palm bends far over in a cyclone and often stands up again.
A car's springs bend over a bump, so the car does not crack.
explanations.art: A tall bamboo bending in a strong wind beside a dry stick snapping.
explanations.context: Is it better to be stiff or to bend? This card explains why bending and springing back can be stronger than being stiff.

explanations.concept: The Earth is springy: earthquakes and a ringing planet
explanations.definition: Rock is elastic too. Deep underground, huge blocks of rock are slowly bent by moving land. When they suddenly slip, they spring back, and the ground shakes. That is an earthquake.
explanations.description: The Earth's outer layer is broken into giant pieces that move slowly, about as fast as your fingernails grow. Where two pieces rub, the rock gets stuck and slowly bends, like a ruler pressed at one end. For years nothing happens. Then the rock slips and springs back in seconds. Harry Fielding Reid, an American scientist, explained this in 1910. He studied the great San Francisco earthquake of 1906. The shaking travels through the Earth as waves, and those waves can travel only because rock is elastic. After a giant earthquake in Chile in 1960, instruments found the whole Earth vibrating slowly, like a struck bell, for days.
examples: The Himalayas are still being pushed up, which is why north India has earthquakes.
Bend a plastic ruler slowly until it slips off your finger. It springs back with a twang, like rock in an earthquake.
explanations.art: A cut-away of the ground with two blocks of rock bent like a pressed ruler, then springing back with shaking lines above.
explanations.context: Can the ground stretch and spring back like a rubber band? This card shows how the bending of rock causes earthquakes.

explanations.definition: Space can stretch and squeeze. When huge things like black holes crash together, they send out ripples in space called gravitational waves.
explanations.description: Albert Einstein predicted these ripples in 1916. As a wave passes, space stretches one way and squeezes the other way, then back again. On 14 September 2015, two giant instruments in the United States, called LIGO, caught one for the first time. It came from two black holes that crashed together more than a billion years ago. The wave stretched LIGO's 4-kilometre-long arms by less than a thousandth of the width of a proton, a speck inside an atom. More than a thousand scientists worked on it, including teams from India. India is now building its own detector, called LIGO-India, in Maharashtra. The whole universe is stretching too. Galaxies are slowly getting further apart, because the space between them is growing.
examples: Draw dots on a wide rubber band and stretch it. Every dot moves away from every other dot, a little like galaxies in our growing universe.
A gravitational wave passing through you right now would stretch you a tiny bit taller and thinner, then shorter and wider.
explanations.art: Two black holes spiralling together, sending rings of stretched and squeezed space across a grid towards a tiny Earth.
explanations.context: Stretching is not only for rubber bands. This card is about space itself stretching and squeezing.

explanations.concept: What is space, that it can stretch?
explanations.description: We know space can stretch, squeeze and ripple. We have measured it. But what is space made of, that it can do this? Is it a kind of stuff, like the rubber of a rubber band? Or is stretching just a way of describing distances between things changing? Nobody knows for sure. This is one of the deepest open questions in physics.
examples: A rubber sheet with a heavy ball on it is often used to picture bent space. It is a helpful picture, but space is not really a rubber sheet.

perspectives.who: Einstein's theory of gravity, called general relativity
perspectives.explanation: Space and time together bend, stretch and ripple. The theory describes this very well. It does not say what space is made of.

perspectives.who: Some physicists working on string theory
perspectives.explanation: Everything might be made of incredibly tiny vibrating strings, a little like plucked rubber bands. Space itself might come from them. Nobody has found any evidence yet that this is true.

perspectives.who: Other physicists, working on ideas like loop quantum gravity
perspectives.explanation: Space might be made of tiny pieces, like the threads of a woven net, far too small to ever see. This idea also has no evidence yet.

explanations.art: A child holding a stretched rubber band up to a starry sky, with a question mark made of rippling grid lines.
explanations.context: Scientists have measured space stretching. This card asks a question nobody can yet answer: what is space, that it can stretch?

agreed.text: Elastic things change shape when pushed or pulled, and go back when the force stops.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can test this with rubber bands, springs and sponges. Engineers test steel, wood and concrete the same way, with big machines that stretch and squash them.

agreed.text: For many springs, double the pull gives about double the stretch, up to a limit.
agreed.evidence: Robert Hooke tested springs and wires and published the rule in 1678. Forcemeters and spring balances work because of it. Children repeat this test with coins and rubber bands.

chart.title: Made-up example: length of a rubber band as coins are added
chart.note: Each 5 coins made the band about 1 cm longer. The line is straight.

agreed.text: Every elastic thing has a limit. Past it, the thing stays stretched or breaks.
agreed.evidence: Stretch a pen spring hard and it stays long. Engineers measure the limit of every material used in bridges and buildings.

agreed.text: A stretched or squashed elastic thing stores energy, which it gives back when it springs back.
agreed.evidence: Catapults, bows, wind-up clocks and bouncing balls all use it. Scientists measure the energy that goes in and comes out.

agreed.text: Earthquakes happen when bent rock underground suddenly slips and springs back.
agreed.evidence: Scientists measured how the ground had bent before and after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake. Today they measure the slow bending with satellites.

challenging.claim: Stretchy things are weak, and strong things are stiff.
challenging.for: A rubber band breaks easily, while a steel rod does not stretch at all that we can see.
challenging.against: Spider silk is very stretchy and, weight for weight, stronger than steel wire. Living roots and bamboo survive storms because they bend. Being able to stretch can make a thing tougher, because it soaks up a sudden push instead of cracking.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that only stiff things can be strong.

challenging.claim: Robert Hooke alone discovered the rule for springs, and invented the spring for watches.
challenging.for: Hooke published the spring rule in 1678. He also worked on springs to control watches in the 1660s.
challenging.against: Christiaan Huygens, a Dutch scientist, built a watch with a spiral spring in 1675. The two men argued bitterly about who was first. Hooke had hidden his rule in a code of jumbled letters in 1676, so that nobody could steal it before he was ready. Historians still disagree about the watch spring. The spring rule is fairly given to Hooke.
challenging.context: This card is about who gets the credit for discovering how springs work.

challenging.claim: Isaac Newton had the only portrait of Robert Hooke destroyed.
challenging.who: A story often told about Hooke and Newton, who were rivals
challenging.for: No portrait of Hooke survives from his lifetime. Newton disliked Hooke, and he led the Royal Society, the science club where a portrait might have hung.
challenging.against: Nobody has found any evidence that Newton destroyed a portrait. It may simply have been lost. In the 2000s an artist, Rita Greer, painted new portraits of Hooke from written descriptions of him.
challenging.context: Robert Hooke found the rule for how springs stretch. This card is about a story of why we do not know what he looked like.

challenging.claim: Rubber was invented in Europe or America, by people like Charles Goodyear.
challenging.for: Charles Goodyear found in 1839 how to make rubber tough with heat and sulphur. That made car tyres and rubber bands possible.
challenging.against: About 3,500 years ago, people in Mexico and Central America were already making bouncy rubber balls. In 1999, Dorothy Hosler and her team at MIT showed how. They mixed the milky sap of the rubber tree with juice from a morning glory vine. Different mixtures made rubber that bounced more, or rubber that was tougher.
challenging.context: This card is about who first made rubber, the stuff of rubber bands and bouncy balls.

challenging.claim: Cold would not matter to the rubber seals on the space shuttle Challenger.
challenging.who: Managers at NASA and at the company that made the rockets, in January 1986
challenging.for: The seals had worked on earlier flights. The managers were under pressure to launch on time.
challenging.against: An engineer called Roger Boisjoly warned the night before that cold rubber goes stiff and springs back too slowly. The launch went ahead on a freezing morning. A seal failed, and the shuttle broke apart. The seven astronauts on board died. Later, the scientist Richard Feynman dipped a piece of the seal rubber in iced water during the inquiry. It stayed squashed instead of springing back.
challenging.context: This card is a sad true story. It shows why it matters how fast rubber springs back, and why it matters to listen to people who warn us.

challenging.claim: A branch that is bending is about to break.
challenging.for: Branches do break when they are bent too far.
challenging.against: Bending by itself is safe. A green branch bends in every breeze and springs back. The warning sign is a branch that bends and does not come all the way back. That means it has passed its elastic limit. Engineers watch for this same sign in cranes and bridges.
challenging.context: This card is about how to tell when something that bends is in danger, and when it is fine.

big_questions.q: Why does a rubber band come back when you let go? How does it 'remember' its shape?
big_questions.hint: Think of tangled noodles being pulled straight. What happens when you let go of them in a bowl that keeps shaking?

big_questions.q: Is anything completely stiff? Does a brick stretch even a tiny bit when you stand on it?
big_questions.hint: Every solid is made of atoms joined by bonds that act like tiny springs.

big_questions.q: When you stretch a catapult, where does the energy go while you are holding it? Where does it go after you let go?
big_questions.hint: Hold a stretched band to your forehead. Then think about the flying paper ball.

big_questions.q: Is it better to be stiff or to bend? Think of trees in a storm, bridges and people.
big_questions.hint: Bamboo bends in a storm. A dry twig snaps. When have you bent instead of breaking?

big_questions.q: If you stretch too far, you don't come back. Is that true for people too? How do you know when you are near your limit?
big_questions.hint: What happens to a rubber band that is stretched round a bundle for months? What helps it rest?

big_questions.q: A rubber band can be stretched and come back thousands of times. Does anything last for ever, or does everything wear out in the end?
big_questions.hint: Look at an old rubber band. What has changed?

big_questions.q: Space itself stretches. What could space be made of?
big_questions.hint: Nobody knows. What would you guess, and how could anyone ever test it?

big_questions.q: People in Mexico made bouncy rubber 3,500 years ago, but the books often credit someone else. Why do some inventors get remembered and others get forgotten?
big_questions.hint: Who wrote the books? Who was allowed to write?

big_questions.q: An engineer warned that cold rubber would not spring back in time, and nobody listened. Why is it hard to listen to someone who says 'stop'?
big_questions.hint: Think of a time you wanted something to go ahead, and someone warned you.

big_questions.q: A flea, a kangaroo and you all use springs to jump. Why might living things have ended up so full of springs?
big_questions.hint: A spring gives back the energy you put in. Why would that help an animal that runs or jumps every day?

big_questions.q: In the story, Ammu spoke up even though the others laughed. Why is it hard to say 'stop' when everyone is having fun?
big_questions.hint: What did Ammu know that the others did not? What made her brave?

story.title: The Tired Branch
story.note: Rubber tapping in Kerala, smoked rubber sheets and the Onam swing, the oonjal, are real. Ammu, her family, Biju and the mango tree are made up. The warning sign in the story is real physics: a branch or spring that no longer springs all the way back has gone past its elastic limit, and may soon break.
text: In a village near Kottayam, in Kerala, the rubber trees stand in long straight rows, like children lined up for school. Every morning before the sun was up, Ammu's mother walked between them with a lamp on her forehead and a curved knife in her hand. On each tree she shaved a thin spiral strip of bark. Out of the cut crept a white, slow milk, which ran down the spiral into a coconut-shell cup. Latex, her mother called it. Rubber before it knows it is rubber.

Ammu was ten. Her job came after school. She carried the full cups home, poured the latex into flat trays and helped her mother squeeze it into sheets through the iron rollers in the shed. Then the sheets were hung in the smoke above the fire to dry, brown and shining, like enormous dosas.

Before any sheet was sold, her mother tested it. She took one corner between her finger and thumb and pulled. A good sheet stretched, and then, when she let go, slid back flat as if nothing had happened. Once Ammu found an old sheet that had been forgotten in the sun for weeks. When her mother pulled it, it stretched and stayed stretched, a tired little bulge. When she pulled again, it tore.
'See,' said her mother. 'When it stops coming back, it is close to breaking.'
Ammu said yes, Amma, the way you say yes to things you are not really listening to. It was August, and Onam was coming, and Onam meant the swing.

Every year the children of the lane hung an oonjal, a festival swing, from the big mango tree at the end of the path. It was a plank seat on two long ropes, decorated with marigolds and mango leaves. This year Biju, who was twelve and the leader of everything, had a plan. 'The low branch is for babies,' he said. 'We'll use the high one. The swing will go up past the roof of the shed.'
The high branch was thinner. It stuck out over the path like an arm reaching for something. Biju climbed up and knotted the ropes round it, and everyone cheered.

On the first day, the swing was glorious. When Biju swung, the branch bent down under him like a fishing rod, and lifted him up again, so that every swing had an extra bounce at the bottom. The children shrieked. They queued all afternoon. Ammu had three turns. At the top of each one she could see over the shed and across the whole green sea of rubber trees, and her stomach floated up into her throat.
On the second day, the bigger boys started swinging two at a time, standing up, pumping as hard as they could. 'Higher!' they yelled. 'Make it fly!'
Ammu was waiting her turn when she noticed something. When the two boys jumped off, the swing hung still. And the branch did not go all the way back up.

She looked again. In the morning, the swing's plank had hung level with her chin. Now it hung level with her shoulder. The branch had bent and stayed bent, just a little, the way the old rubber sheet had stretched and stayed stretched.
She went cold all over, even in the August heat.
'Biju,' she said. 'The branch is tired.'
Biju laughed. Everyone laughed. 'Branches don't get tired,' he said. 'It bounced me all day yesterday.'
'It bounced back yesterday,' said Ammu. 'It isn't bouncing back now. Look at the seat. It's lower.'

'You're scared because you're small,' said one of the boys, and the others made chicken noises. Ammu's face went hot. She wanted to be quiet. Being quiet would have been much easier. But she thought of the old sheet, the tired bulge, and the sound it made when it tore.
Her little sister Kunju was next in the queue, holding up her arms to be lifted on.
'No,' said Ammu, and she pulled Kunju back by her frock, so hard that Kunju began to cry.
'Fine,' said Biju. 'Then I'll show you.' He climbed onto the plank, stood up, and pumped once, twice, three times, swinging higher than the shed roof.
On the fourth swing there was a sound like a coconut splitting.

The branch did not snap all at once. It cracked, and sagged, and Biju, at the bottom of the swing, felt the ropes go soft in his hands. He jumped. He landed on his knees in the mud of the path. A second later the whole branch, ropes, marigolds and all, came down with a heavy, leafy crash exactly where Kunju would have been sitting.
Nobody said anything for a long time. A crow, offended, flew off into the rubber trees.
Biju stood up slowly. His knees were muddy and his face was white. He looked at the broken branch, with its pale, splintered end. Then he looked at Ammu.
'How did you know?' he said.

Ammu told him about the sheet. She showed him how the swing had hung lower and lower. 'When something stops coming back,' she said, 'it's near the end.' She didn't say 'I told you.' She didn't need to.

That evening, Ammu's mother walked down the lane and looked at the branch on the ground. She looked at the high stump, and at the low, thick branch that the swing had always hung from before. She did not scold anyone. She only touched Ammu's head on her way home, very lightly.

The next morning, the children hung the swing again, on the low branch. It was not as exciting. It did not go higher than the shed. But after every turn, Ammu watched the seat as the rider jumped off, and every time, the branch lifted it back up to exactly the height of her chin.
On Onam day, Biju pushed Kunju on the swing himself, gently, for nearly an hour.
story.epiphany: For the parent: a branch, like a rubber band or a spring, is elastic. Pushed a little, it bends and springs all the way back. Pushed past its elastic limit, it bends and stays bent. That small bend that does not come back is the warning. The thing has started to change inside, and it is close to breaking. Ammu spots this because she has seen the same thing in an old rubber sheet. Engineers watch for this sign in bridges, cranes and aeroplane wings. The story also asks how hard it is to speak up when others laugh, and to listen when someone warns us.
ask: How did Ammu's mother test a rubber sheet? What did it mean when the sheet stayed stretched?
What did Ammu notice about the swing seat after the big boys jumped off?
Why did the branch break on the second day, but not on the first?
Why was it hard for Ammu to speak up? What helped her?
Have you ever seen something that 'stopped coming back'? A rubber band, a spring or a toy? What happened to it next?
