Brown rubber sheets hanging in the smoke of a shed, and Ammu's mother pulling a corner of one between finger and thumb.
An Onam swing decorated with marigolds hanging from a high, thin mango branch, children queueing below.
Ammu staring at the empty swing seat, which now hangs at her shoulder, the branch bent lower than before.
The branch cracking and falling with its ropes and flowers, Biju landing in the mud, Ammu holding her little sister back.
The swing hung again from the low, thick branch, Ammu watching the seat rise back to the height of her chin.

games.title: Spring Back, Stay or Snap?
games.players: 2 to 5 players, or one child playing against the app

printables.title: 24 thing cards to cut out
items: TEST IT: stretch a rubber band a little and let go. What does it do?
TEST IT: squeeze a ball of atta dough. Does it spring back?
TEST IT: bend a plastic ruler a little and let go. Then put it away. Don't bend it till it snaps!
TEST IT: pinch the skin on the back of your hand and let go. Watch it.

rules: Cut out the 24 cards. Shuffle them and put them in a pile, face down.
On your turn, take the top card and read it out loud.
Decide: if you stretch, squash or bend this thing, will it spring back, stay changed, or snap? Put the card on that mat.
Then name one place where that thing is useful because it behaves that way. A good idea wins one spring token.
If you draw a TEST IT card, everyone does the test together. The first person to explain the result wins two tokens.
When the cards run out, the player with the most tokens wins.

setup.art: Three paper mats on the floor labelled SPRING BACK, STAY and SNAP, with a pile of face-down cards in the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the three mats and put the cards in a pile.

setup.art: A child holding a card that says 'Rubber band' over the SPRING BACK mat.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card and put it on a mat.

setup.art: Children doing a TEST IT card, one stretching a rubber band, one pressing dough.
setup.caption: 3. TEST IT cards: everyone tries it.

flow.do: 1. Lay the three mats on the floor: SPRING BACK, STAY and SNAP. 2. Shuffle the 24 cards and put them face down in a pile. 3. Put the spring tokens in a bowl.
flow.say: Some things spring back when you stretch or squash them. Scientists call them elastic. Some stay changed, like playdough. Some just snap, like a dry twig. Each card is a thing. We decide which mat it belongs on.
flow.kid: Put the three mats on the floor. Spring back, stay, and snap. Mix up the cards. Put them face down. For each card, pick a mat.
flow.context: This is the first step of Spring Back, Stay or Snap?. It is a card game about which things are elastic. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Find the card 'Pen spring, pulled very hard'. Play it together as a practice round.
flow.say: Let's practise with a tricky one. A pen spring, pulled very hard. Does it spring back, stay, or snap?
flow.kid: Practice card: a pen spring, pulled very hard. Spring back, stay or snap? Tap your answer.

ask.q: Why does a spring pulled very hard stay long?
good: It was stretched too far, so it can't come back.

check.q: A pen spring pulled very hard. Which mat does it go on?
check.why: Game moment: STAY is right. Pulled gently, the spring would go on SPRING BACK. Pulled very hard, it passes its elastic limit and stays long. Picking SNAP usually means 'too far' is pictured as always breaking. Springs usually stretch out first.

flow.parent: The same spring pulled gently goes on SPRING BACK. This shows that one thing can be elastic up to a limit, and then stay changed.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. Each player draws a card, reads it out and puts it on a mat. 2. They name a place where that behaviour is useful. 3. Give one token for each good idea.
flow.say: When you put your card down, tell me where it is useful that this thing springs back, or stays, or snaps.
flow.kid: Take turns. Read your card. Put it on a mat. Then say where that is useful. Each good idea wins a 🌀 token.
flow.parent: Good ideas: a hair band must spring back, or it would fall off. Playdough must stay, or you could not make shapes. A papad snapping is how you know it is crisp. Some cards are tricky. A sponge springs back. Crumpled foil stays. A spider web springs back, which is how it catches flies without breaking.

flow.do: When a TEST IT card comes up, stop and do the test together. Everyone guesses first.
flow.say: Before we test it, everyone guess what will happen. Then we'll try it and see who was right.
flow.kid: A TEST IT card! First, guess what will happen. Then try it. Were you right?

ask.q: You pinched the skin on your hand. Why did it spring back?
good: It has stretchy stuff inside it, called elastin.

flow.think: Can one thing be on two mats? When?

flow.do: 1. Count everyone's tokens to find the winner. 2. Then look at the three piles together.
flow.say: Look at the three piles. Which pile is biggest? Which things were the hardest to decide?
flow.kid: Count your tokens. Who won? Now look at the piles. Which things were hard to decide? Why?
flow.think: Steel, glass and stone are a little elastic too. Do you think anything is never elastic at all?

games.context: This is a card game about elastic things. Elastic means a thing springs back to its shape when you let go. For each thing on a card, players decide: does it spring back, stay changed, or snap?

games.title: Human Springs
games.players: 2 to 6 players, with one grown-up as the caller

printables.title: 16 caller cards
items: STIFF SPRING: move only half as far
FLOPPY SPRING: move twice as far
COLD RUBBER: spring back very slowly
TOO FAR! You pass your limit and stay where you are
TOO FAR! You snap and sit down
STORE IT: crouch and hold, then jump on 'Let go!'

rules: Each player is a spring. Stand on a spot marked with a chappal. That is your resting place.
The caller reads a card. For each gentle pull, the spring takes one step forward. For each gentle push, it takes one step back.
On 'Let go!', every spring jumps back to its resting place.
Special cards change the rules for one round, like STIFF SPRING or TOO FAR.
A spring that moves the wrong number of steps sits out one round. Play until every card has been read.

setup.art: Children standing in a line, each beside a chappal on the floor marking their resting place.
setup.caption: 1. Each spring stands by its chappal.

setup.art: A grown-up reading a card while a child takes two big steps forward.
setup.caption: 2. The caller reads a card. Springs move that many steps.

setup.art: The children jumping back to their chappals as the caller shouts 'Let go!'.
setup.caption: 3. On 'Let go!', everyone springs back.

flow.do: 1. Put one chappal on the floor for each player, in a line with space in front. 2. Each player stands beside a chappal. 3. Shuffle the caller cards.
flow.say: You are all springs. Your chappal is where you rest. When I pull, you stretch forward. When I push, you squash back. When I say 'Let go', you spring home.
flow.kid: You are a spring! Stand by your chappal. That is your home. A pull means step forward. Let go means jump home.
flow.context: This is the first step of Human Springs, an acting game. Each player pretends to be a spring that stretches, squashes and springs back. The founder of DeepKids suggested this game.

flow.do: Read the cards one at a time. Check that each spring moves the right number of steps: one pull, one step.
flow.say: Two gentle pulls! Now let go! Did everyone spring all the way home?
flow.kid: Listen to the caller. One pull, one step. Two pulls, two steps. Let go means jump home!

ask.q: Three pulls made you move three steps. What would six pulls do?

flow.parent: This acts out the spring rule: double the pull, double the stretch. Robert Hooke wrote this rule down in 1678.

flow.do: Read the special cards: STIFF SPRING, FLOPPY SPRING, COLD RUBBER, TOO FAR and STORE IT.
flow.say: Too far! You've passed your limit. When I say let go, you can't get home. You stay where you are.
flow.kid: Special card! A stiff spring moves only a little. Too far means you can't get home. Act it out!

check.q: A spring is pulled TOO FAR, past its limit. When you let go, what happens?
options: It springs all the way back
It stays stretched, or it snaps
check.why: Game moment: a spring pulled past its limit cannot get home. It stays stretched or snaps. Picking 'springs all the way back' means elastic was thought to have no limit. Picking 'shorter' mixes up stretching with squashing.

flow.parent: COLD RUBBER links to a true story. Cold rubber springs back slowly. That mattered on the space shuttle Challenger in 1986. Tell it only if your child is ready for a sad story.

flow.do: Finish with STORE IT and BOUNCE. Everyone crouches, holds, then jumps on 'Let go!'.
flow.say: Crouch down and hold it. You are a squashed spring, full of stored energy. Let go!
flow.kid: Crouch low and hold. You are a squashed spring. Wait for it. Let go! Jump!
flow.think: When you crouch before a jump, your legs are like springs. Where in your body are the springs?

games.context: This is an acting game. Each child is a spring. They stretch when the caller pulls, squash when the caller pushes, and spring back home on 'Let go!'.

items.p: What does elastic mean?
opts: It changes shape when pushed or pulled, and springs back when you let go
items.why: Elastic things spring back to their old shape. Picking 'soft' is a common idea, but steel springs are hard and still elastic. Picking 'made of rubber' misses springs, sponges and skin.
items.art: A rubber band stretched and then back to normal.

items.p: Which of these is elastic?
items.why: A hair band springs back. Playdough and wet clay stay changed. A papad snaps. Picking playdough often means 'it changes shape' was mixed up with 'it springs back'. Elastic needs both.

items.p: A thing that springs back after being stretched is called ____.
items.why: Elastic things, like rubber bands, go back to their old shape when you let go.

items.p: Sort these. Do they spring back, stay changed, or snap?
items.why: Sponges and rubber bands are elastic. Playdough and gum keep their new shape. Twigs and glass hardly bend before they break.

items.p: In the coin stretch test, you add more coins to the cup. What happens to the rubber band?
items.why: More coins pull down harder, so the band stretches more. Picking 'shorter' sometimes comes from thinking the band 'fights back' and pulls itself up. It does pull back, but it still gets longer.
items.context: In the coin stretch test, you hang a paper cup from a rubber band and add coins, 5 at a time.

items.p: Steel is a little bit elastic.
items.why: True. Steel springs back too. It just needs a much bigger force to stretch or bend it. That is why springs are made of steel.

items.p: You can stretch a spring as far as you like, and it will always spring back.
items.why: False. Every spring has an elastic limit. Pull it past that and it stays stretched, or it breaks.

items.p: A pen spring was pulled very hard. Now it stays long and loose. Why?
opts: It went past its elastic limit
items.why: Past the elastic limit, a spring stays stretched. Picking 'never elastic' misses that it did spring back when pulled gently.
items.context: In the Find the Limit experiment, you stretch different things and measure them before and after.

items.p: Match each spring to its job.
items.why: Springs are used wherever something must push or pull back, or soak up a bump.

items.p: You squash the pen spring all the way down and let go. Then you squash it only halfway. Which jumps higher?
items.why: Squashing more stores more energy, so it jumps higher. Picking 'both the same' often means the spring is pictured as having one fixed jump. In fact the jump depends on how much you squash it.
items.context: In the Pen Spring Jump, you squash the small spring from a clicky pen beside a ruler, and let it jump.

items.p: Why does a ball of dough not bounce?
opts: It is not elastic, so it squashes and stays squashed
items.why: A bounce is a squash and a spring back. Dough squashes but does not spring back. Picking 'too heavy' is a common guess. But a heavy rubber ball still bounces.

items.p: A stretched catapult stores ____, which flings the paper ball when you let go.
items.why: Stretching an elastic thing stores energy. Letting go gives it back as movement.

items.p: Which part of your body works like a spring when you jump?
opts: The tendon at the back of your ankle
items.why: Your Achilles tendon stretches as you land and springs back as you push off. Hair is a little stretchy too, but it does not help you jump.

items.p: Name two springs or elastic things in your home. Say what job each one does.
items.a: Any two good examples, each with a job. For example: the spring in my pen pushes the tip back in. The elastic in my socks stops them falling down.
items.why: Any two correct examples, each with a job, are right.

items.p: Draw a rubber band before and after you stretch it. Draw an arrow to show which way it pulls back on your fingers.
items.a: Two drawings: a small loop, then a long loop. The pull-back arrows point inwards, towards the middle of the band.
items.why: A stretched band pulls back towards its old shape. That pull-back force points inwards.
items.art: Two fingers holding a stretched band, with space for arrows.

items.p: Look at the line graph from the coin stretch test. With 0 coins the band was 10 cm. With 10 coins it was 12 cm. How long was it with 20 coins?
items.why: Each 5 coins added 1 cm. 20 coins is 4 lots of 5, so the band grew 4 cm. 10 + 4 = 14 cm. Picking 20 cm usually means the coins were counted as centimetres.

chart.title: Made-up example: length of a rubber band as coins are added
chart.note: Each 5 coins made the band about 1 cm longer. The line is straight.

items.context: In the coin stretch test, you hang a paper cup from a rubber band and add coins, 5 at a time. You measure the band each time.

items.p: The line on the coin stretch graph is straight. What does that tell us?
opts: Each 5 coins added the same extra length
items.why: A straight line means the same change each step. This is the spring rule: double the pull, about double the stretch. Picking 'did not stretch' mixes up a flat line with a straight sloping line.

chart.title: Made-up example: length of a rubber band as coins are added
chart.note: Each 5 coins made the band about 1 cm longer. The line is straight.

items.p: A thick rubber band and a thin one hold the same coins. The thick one stretches less. What do scientists call the thick band?
items.why: A stiff spring needs a bigger pull to stretch the same amount. Picking 'weaker' is a common idea. In fact the thick band can usually hold more before it snaps.

items.p: Look at the bounce test chart. Which ball is the most elastic?
items.why: The rubber ball bounced back highest, 80 cm out of 100 cm. It springs back best and loses the least energy. Picking the sponge ball often means soft is thought to be springy. Soft is not the same as elastic.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how high each ball bounced back from 1 metre
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your balls will be different.

items.context: In the Bounce Test, you drop different balls from 1 metre and measure how high they bounce back.

items.p: A good rubber ball dropped from 1 metre can bounce back higher than 1 metre.
items.why: False. Some energy always turns into heat and sound when it squashes. So it never comes all the way back up, unless someone throws it down.

items.p: Why does a bamboo tree bend in a storm instead of snapping?
opts: It is elastic, so it bends, stores the push, and springs back
items.why: Springy things soak up a sudden push by bending. Picking 'dead inside' is the opposite. Dry, dead wood is the kind that snaps.

items.p: In the story 'The Tired Branch', Ammu saw the swing seat hanging lower after the boys jumped off. What did that tell her?
opts: The branch had passed its elastic limit and might break
The ropes had got longer in the sun
items.why: The branch had bent and stayed bent, so it was no longer springing back. That is the warning sign of the elastic limit. Picking 'the ropes got longer' is a sensible guess, but the branch was what had sagged.
items.context: In this unit's story, children in Kerala hang an Onam swing from a thin, high mango branch and swing on it very hard.

items.p: Ammu's mother pulls the corner of a rubber sheet. An old sheet stretches and stays stretched. What idea does this show?
items.why: A good sheet springs back. An old, sun-damaged sheet stays stretched, because it has passed its limit. Soon it tears. Picking 'friction' mixes up rubbing with stretching.
items.context: In this unit's story, Ammu's mother makes rubber sheets in Kerala. She tests each one by pulling a corner.

items.p: Sort these by what they store energy in.
items.why: A catapult band, a bow string and trampoline springs are stretched. A pen spring and a ball are squashed. The car's band is twisted round the axle.

items.p: The rubber band car went 60 cm with 5 winds and 180 cm with 15 winds. Why?
items.why: Each wind twists the band more and stores more energy. Picking 'lighter' or 'floor changed' means wanting another cause. In a fair test, only the winds changed.
items.context: In the Rubber Band Car project, you twist a rubber band round the back axle by winding the wheels backwards.

items.p: You stretch a rubber band fast and touch it to your forehead. How does it feel?
items.why: Stretching rubber quickly makes it warm. Its tangled chains are pulled straight, and that gives out heat. Picking 'cold' often comes from rubber feeling cool to touch at first. Test it and feel the change.

items.p: Match each living thing to its spring.
items.why: Living things use elastic parts to jump, catch food and stay in one piece.

items.p: Why does your skin spring back after a pinch?
opts: It has a stretchy stuff called elastin
items.why: Elastin is a stretchy material in skin, lungs and blood vessels. Picking 'blood pushes it back' is a sensible guess. But blood moves too slowly to push skin back so fast. Picking 'rubber' is close in spirit, because elastin is rubbery, but it is made by your body.

items.p: A spring balance at a vegetable shop has a spring inside. Why does a heavier bag of onions move the pointer further?
items.a: A heavier bag pulls down harder on the spring. A bigger pull stretches the spring further, so the pointer moves further down the scale.
items.why: The spring rule: a bigger pull makes a bigger stretch. The unit on measuring forces looks at this more.

items.p: Draw the catapult from the Catapult Challenge. Label where the energy is stored before you let go.
items.a: A drawing of the catapult with the arm pressed down. The label points to the bent arm or the stretched rubber bands.
items.why: The bent stick and stretched bands store the energy. When you let go, they spring back and fling the ball.
items.art: An empty box to draw in.

items.p: Deep down, why does a steel spring spring back?
opts: Its atoms are held by electric pulls that act like tiny springs
It has tiny rubber bands inside
items.why: Bonds between atoms pull them back to their places. Picking 'tiny rubber bands' is a nice picture, but there is no rubber in steel. Picking gravity misses that springs work sideways and upside down too.

items.p: Rubber springs back for a different reason. What is rubber made of?
opts: Long tangled chains, like cooked noodles
Neat rows of atoms, like steel
items.why: Rubber is made of polymers, long tangled chains. Stretching straightens them. Jiggling shakes them back into a tangle. Picking 'neat rows' is how steel is built, not rubber.

items.p: Past the elastic limit, a steel spring stays stretched. What happens to its atoms?
opts: Rows of atoms slide into new places and do not slide back
items.why: Below the limit, bonds just stretch. Past it, rows of atoms slip over each other into new places. Picking 'disappear' is a common guess, but atoms are never lost. They only move.

items.p: A stretched rubber band pulls harder when you warm it.
items.why: True. Warmth makes the chains jiggle more, so they pull back into a tangle harder. This is the opposite of most materials. John Gough first noticed rubber's warmth in 1805.

items.p: What causes an earthquake?
opts: Rock slowly bends underground, then suddenly slips and springs back
Heavy buildings press the ground down
items.why: Harry Fielding Reid explained this in 1910. Picking 'heavy buildings' is a common worry, but earthquakes start many kilometres underground, far below any building.
items.context: Rock deep underground is slowly bent as the Earth's giant pieces move.

items.p: In the ruler earthquake, you press a ruler's end down until it slips off your finger. The twang is like…
opts: The shaking when bent rock slips
items.why: The bent ruler stores energy, then lets it all go at once. Bent rock does the same in an earthquake.
items.context: In the Bend or Snap? activity, you hold a ruler on a table and slowly press its free end down until it slips.

items.p: In 2015, LIGO caught a gravitational wave. What did the wave do to LIGO's 4-kilometre arms?
opts: Stretched and squeezed them by far less than the width of an atom
items.why: The stretch was less than a thousandth of the width of a proton, a tiny speck inside an atom. Picking '1 metre' shows how hard it is to imagine something so small. That is why LIGO took decades to build.
items.context: A gravitational wave is a ripple in space itself. It stretches space one way and squeezes it the other way.

items.p: In Rubber Band Galaxies, you stretched a strip with dots on it. Which dot moved furthest from dot A?
items.why: When the whole strip stretches, far dots move away faster. Astronomers see the same with galaxies. Picking 'all the same' misses that each piece of rubber between dots stretches, so more rubber means more stretch.

items.p: Scientists know exactly what space is made of.
items.why: False. We have measured space stretching, but nobody knows what space is made of. String theory and loop quantum gravity are ideas with no evidence yet.

items.p: Who made bouncy rubber balls about 3,500 years ago?
opts: People in ancient Mexico and Central America
items.why: Dorothy Hosler's team showed in 1999 how they mixed rubber-tree sap with morning glory juice. Picking Goodyear is common, because books credit him. He lived about 3,300 years later.

items.p: Why did the cold matter for the rubber seals on the space shuttle Challenger?
opts: Cold rubber springs back too slowly to seal the gap
items.why: Cold rubber goes stiff, so it springs back slowly. The engineer Roger Boisjoly warned about this. Picking 'melts' mixes up cold with heat.
items.context: In January 1986, the space shuttle Challenger launched on a freezing morning. Rubber rings sealed the joints in its rockets.

items.p: Robert Hooke hid his spring rule in a code of jumbled letters in 1676. Why might he have done this?
opts: So nobody could claim it before he was ready to explain it
items.why: Scientists sometimes did this to prove later that they had the idea first. Picking 'a joke' is a fair guess for something so odd. But it was a serious way to protect his claim.

items.p: Spider silk is very stretchy, and weight for weight stronger than steel wire. Does that change the idea that stretchy things are weak? Explain.
items.a: Yes. Spider silk shows that a thing can be both stretchy and strong. Stretching lets it soak up a fly hitting the web without snapping.
items.why: Being able to stretch can make a material tougher, because it soaks up sudden pushes.

items.p: In the bungee doll challenge, 2 bands let the doll fall 30 cm, 3 bands 40 cm and 4 bands 50 cm. Describe the pattern. Then predict 8 bands.
items.a: Each extra band adds 10 cm. 4 bands is 50 cm, so 8 bands is 4 more bands, which is 40 cm more. 50 + 40 = 90 cm.
items.why: The pattern goes up by the same amount each time, like the spring rule. Real rubber bands may curve a little near their limit.

items.p: Is it better to be stiff or to bend? Give one example where stiff is better and one where bending is better.
items.a: A balanced answer. For example: a ruler for drawing lines should be stiff. A bridge in a storm, or a tree, is better if it can bend and spring back.
items.why: There is no single right answer. What counts is a good example for each side.

items.p: Draw a model of atoms in a spring, as balls joined by tiny springs. Draw it again when the spring is stretched.
items.a: Two drawings. In the first, balls are evenly spaced with short springs between them. In the second, the balls are a little further apart and the springs are longer.
items.why: Stretching a spring stretches the bonds between its atoms a tiny bit each.

experiments.title: Thick Band, Thin Band: the coin stretch test
experiments.question: How much longer does a rubber band get for every 5 coins? Does a thick band stretch as much as a thin one?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. With 25 coins in the cup, how long will the thin band be? Will the thick band be longer or shorter than the thin one?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, change only the number of coins. Use the same cup, the same kind of coins and the same ruler. Measure the band the same way every time, from the pencil to the top of the cup. Test the thick band in exactly the same way afterwards.

materials.item: a thin rubber band and a thick rubber band, both about the same length
a small paper cup with a string or paper-clip handle
25 coins of the same kind, such as 1-rupee coins
a pencil, and two chairs or a shelf edge to rest it on
a 30 cm ruler

experiments.safety: Stand to the side, not over the cup, in case the band slips or snaps. Use coins, not glass marbles, in the cup.

schedule.what: Measure the thin band and the thick band with 0 to 25 coins. Draw a line graph.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a line graph for the thin band. Put coins along the bottom and length up the side. Join the dots.

setup.art: A pencil resting across the backs of two chairs, a thin rubber band hanging from it, and an empty paper cup hooked on the band.
setup.caption: 1. Hang the band from a pencil. Hook the cup on the band.

setup.art: A child holding a ruler upright beside the hanging band, reading the length from the pencil down to the cup's handle.
setup.caption: 2. Measure the band before adding coins.

setup.art: A hand dropping 5 coins into the paper cup, the band now a little longer.
setup.caption: 3. Add 5 coins. Measure again.

setup.art: The cup with 25 coins and the band clearly longer, the ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 4. Keep going to 25 coins, then try the thick band.

flow.do: 1. Rest a pencil across the backs of two chairs. 2. Loop the thin rubber band over the pencil. 3. Hook the cup's handle on the bottom of the band.
flow.say: We're going to find out exactly how much a rubber band stretches when we add weight. First, let's hang it up.
flow.kid: Put a pencil across two chairs. Hang the thin band on it. Hook the cup on the band.
flow.context: This is the first step of the coin stretch test. You hang a cup from a rubber band, add coins, and measure how long the band gets.

ask.q: What do you think will happen when we add coins?
good: It will get longer and longer.

flow.do: 1. Hold the ruler upright beside the band, with 0 at the pencil. 2. Read the length to the bottom of the band. 3. Write it in the table next to 0 coins.
flow.say: Let's measure before we add anything. Keep the ruler straight, and look at it from the side, at eye level.
flow.kid: Hold the ruler up straight. Start at the pencil. Read the number at the bottom of the band. Write it down.
flow.parent: Looking from the side, at eye level, gives a true reading. Looking from above or below makes the number look wrong. Half centimetres are fine to write down.

flow.do: 1. Gently drop 5 coins into the cup. 2. Wait until it stops bouncing. 3. Measure and write the length. 4. Repeat until there are 25 coins.
flow.say: Five more coins. How much longer did it get this time? Is it the same as last time?
flow.kid: Add 5 coins. Wait till it stops bouncing. Measure. Write it down. Do it again, up to 25.

ask.q: Did each 5 coins add about the same length?

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: 1. Take all the coins out. 2. Measure the thin band again. 3. Then do the whole test again with the thick band.
flow.say: Now the coins are out. Did the band spring all the way back? Now let's try the thick band in exactly the same way.
flow.kid: Take the coins out. Did the band go back to its first length? Now test the thick band the same way.

check.q: The coins are out. The thin band is back to 10 cm. What does that show?
options: The band is elastic: it sprang back
check.why: The band went back to its first length, so it is elastic. Picking 'broken' usually means stretching was thought to damage it. A small stretch does not. Picking 'heavier' mixes up the coins' weight with the band.

flow.do: Help your child draw a line graph for the thin band. Coins go along the bottom. Length goes up the side. Join the dots.
flow.say: Let's turn the numbers into a picture. Each measurement is a dot. When we join them, what shape do we get?
flow.kid: Draw a dot for each measurement. Coins go along the bottom. Length goes up the side. Join the dots. Is it a straight line?

chart.title: Made-up example: length of a rubber band as coins are added
chart.note: Each 5 coins made the band about 1 cm longer. The line is straight.

flow.parent: For many rubber bands the line is nearly straight. That is the spring rule: double the pull, about double the stretch. Real rubber bands often curve a little, which is fine. Write down what you really saw.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: more coins stretch a band more, and a thick band stretches less. What I saw: each 5 coins made the thin band about 1 cm longer, but the thick band only about half a centimetre longer. Why: more coins pull down harder, and the thick band is stiffer, so it needs a bigger pull to stretch.

experiments.context: This is the coin stretch test. You hang a paper cup from a rubber band and add coins, 5 at a time. You measure the band each time. Then you test a thicker band the same way.

experiments.title: Pen Spring Jump
experiments.question: If you squash a spring more, does it jump higher?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will a spring squashed all the way jump higher, lower or the same as a spring squashed halfway?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same spring every time, on the same table, beside the same ruler. Change only how much you squash it. Try each squash 3 times, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: the spring from an old clicky ballpoint pen
a 30 cm ruler, taped upright to a wall or a box
tape

experiments.safety: A grown-up takes the spring out of the pen. Keep faces back from the spring when it jumps. Never point it at anyone.

schedule.what: Squash the spring halfway and all the way, let it jump, and measure how high it goes.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then write one sentence about which squash made the spring jump higher.

setup.art: A grown-up unscrewing a clicky pen and taking out its small spring.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up takes the spring out of an old pen.

setup.art: A ruler taped upright against a wall at the edge of a table, the small spring standing beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Tape a ruler upright. Stand the spring beside it.

setup.art: A finger pressing the spring halfway down, then sliding off so the spring jumps up beside the ruler.
setup.caption: 3. Squash it, slide your finger off, and watch how high it jumps.

flow.do: 1. Unscrew an old clicky pen and take out the spring. 2. Tape a ruler upright against a wall at the edge of the table, with 0 at the bottom.
flow.say: There's a spring hiding inside this pen. Let's take it out and see what it can do.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to open an old clicky pen. Find the spring inside. Stand it beside the ruler.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Pen Spring Jump. You squash the little spring from a clicky pen and see how high it jumps.

flow.do: 1. Squash the spring halfway with one finger. 2. Slide your finger off sideways, quickly. 3. Watch the ruler and see how high the top of the spring goes. 4. Do it 3 times and write each height.
flow.say: Squash it halfway. Now slide your finger off fast. How high did it get? Your eyes need to be at the ruler.
flow.kid: Squash the spring halfway. Slide your finger off fast. How high did it jump? Write it down. Try 3 times.
flow.parent: The jump is quick. A phone video in slow motion helps a lot. Or one person watches the ruler while the other releases the spring.

flow.do: Now squash the spring all the way down, and do the same 3 times.
flow.say: Now squash it all the way. Where does the extra jump come from?
flow.kid: Now squash it all the way down. Let go the same way. Measure 3 times. Higher or lower?

ask.q: Why did the fully squashed spring jump higher?
good: It was squashed more, so it pushed back harder.

check.q: The spring squashed all the way jumped higher. Why?
options: It stored more energy when squashed more
check.why: Squashing more stores more energy, and the spring gives it back as a higher jump. Picking 'lighter' or 'the ruler moved' means looking for another cause. In a fair test, only the squash changed.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: squashing a spring more makes it jump higher. What I saw: squashed halfway, it jumped about 8 cm. Squashed all the way, it jumped about 20 cm. Why: the more you squash it, the more energy it stores, and it gives that energy back when it springs.

experiments.context: In this experiment you take the small spring out of a clicky pen. You squash it a little or a lot, let go, and measure how high it jumps beside a ruler.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: how high the pen spring jumped
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your spring will be different.

experiments.title: Find the Limit
experiments.question: When we stretch or bend different things, which spring back, which stay changed, and which snap?
experiments.predict: Before you test each thing, guess. Will it spring back, stay changed, or snap?
experiments.fair_test: Measure each thing before you stretch it. Stretch each one to about twice its length, or bend it gently, then let go. Measure it again straight away. That way you compare each thing with itself.

materials.item: a rubber band
a strip cut from a thin plastic carry bag, about 10 cm long and 2 cm wide
an old pen spring
a rope of playdough or atta dough, about 10 cm long
a stick of uncooked spaghetti or a thin dry twig
a ruler

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the plastic strip. Bend the spaghetti away from your face. Throw away the plastic strip safely afterwards, so animals cannot eat it.

schedule.what: Measure, stretch and measure again: five things.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Circle the things that sprang back. Draw the pen spring before and after a very hard pull.

setup.art: Five things in a row on a table with a ruler: a rubber band, a plastic strip, a pen spring, a rope of dough and a stick of spaghetti.
setup.caption: 1. Line up the five things and measure each one.

setup.art: Two hands stretching the plastic strip to twice its length beside a ruler.
setup.caption: 2. Stretch each one to about twice its length.

setup.art: The plastic strip lying long and thin after being let go, beside the rubber band which is back to its first size.
setup.caption: 3. Let go. Measure it again.

setup.art: Two hands gently bending a stick of uncooked spaghetti until it snaps.
setup.caption: 4. Bend the spaghetti gently. What happens?

flow.do: 1. Line up the five things. 2. Measure each one and write its length in the table. 3. Write your child's guess for each.
flow.say: Let's guess first. For each thing: will it spring back, stay stretched, or snap?
flow.kid: Measure each thing. Write the length. Then guess: spring back, stay, or snap?
flow.context: This is the first step of Find the Limit. You stretch or bend five different things and see which spring back. Elastic things spring back. Every elastic thing has a limit.

flow.do: 1. Stretch the rubber band, plastic strip, pen spring and dough to about twice their length. 2. Let go. 3. Measure each one again straight away. 4. Gently bend the spaghetti until it bends a little, then more.
flow.say: Stretch it to twice as long. Let go. Now measure. Is it the same as before?
flow.kid: Stretch each one to twice as long. Let go. Measure again. Bend the spaghetti gently. What happens?
flow.parent: Expect this. The rubber band springs back. The plastic strip stays long and thin. The dough stays long. The pen spring springs back if pulled gently, but stays long if pulled hard. The spaghetti bends a tiny bit, then snaps.

flow.do: Pull the old pen spring very hard, far past twice its length. Let go and measure.
flow.say: Now let's pull the spring too far on purpose. Watch what happens when we let go.
flow.kid: Pull the old pen spring very hard. Let go. Did it come back? Measure it.

check.q: The pen spring was pulled very hard. Now it stays long and loose. Why?
options: It was pulled past its elastic limit
Springs always get longer over time
check.why: It went past its elastic limit, so rows of atoms slipped into new places. Picking 'never elastic' misses that it sprang back when pulled gently. Picking 'always get longer' mixes it up with wearing out slowly.

flow.think: The plastic strip and the spring both stayed long. Deep down, rows of atoms slid into new places. Can they slide back?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: elastic things spring back, but only up to a limit. What I saw: the rubber band went back to 6 cm. The plastic strip went from 10 cm to 18 cm and stayed. The spaghetti snapped. The pen spring came back when I pulled it a little, but stayed long when I pulled it hard. Why: every elastic thing has a limit, and past it, it stays changed or breaks.

experiments.context: In this experiment you stretch or bend five things: a rubber band, a plastic strip, a pen spring, dough and spaghetti. You measure them before and after, to see which spring back, which stay changed and which snap.

experiments.title: The Bounce Test
experiments.question: Which ball bounces highest when dropped from the same height?
experiments.predict: Line up the balls. Put the one you think will bounce highest first, and the one you think will bounce lowest last.
experiments.fair_test: Drop every ball from the same height, 1 metre, onto the same hard floor. Let go without pushing it down. Drop each ball 3 times and take the middle value.

materials.item: 3 or 4 different balls, for example a rubber ball, a tennis ball, a plastic ball and a sponge ball
a ball of atta dough, the size of a lemon
a metre scale, or a 1-metre strip of paper taped to a wall and marked every 10 cm

experiments.safety: Do this on a clear, hard floor away from glass. Put the dough ball on a plate afterwards for cooking or composting.

schedule.what: Drop each ball from 1 metre 3 times and measure the bounce. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart, with one bar for each ball's middle value.

setup.art: A paper strip marked every 10 cm taped to a wall from the floor up to 1 metre, with balls lined up on the floor below.
setup.caption: 1. Tape a 1-metre strip to the wall.

setup.art: A child holding a tennis ball level with the 1-metre mark, about to let go.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the ball at the 1-metre mark. Let go.

setup.art: A grown-up crouching with eyes level with the strip, watching the top of the bounce.
setup.caption: 3. Watch how high the ball bounces back.

setup.art: A ball of dough flattened on the floor, not bouncing.
setup.caption: 4. Try the dough ball too.

flow.do: 1. Tape the strip to a wall, from the floor up. 2. Ask your child to put the balls in a line, highest bouncer first.
flow.say: Which ball do you think will bounce highest? Put them in a line.
flow.kid: Put the balls in a line. Which will bounce highest? Put that one first.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bounce Test. You drop different balls from 1 metre and measure how high each one bounces back.

ask.q: Why did you put that one first?

flow.do: 1. Hold a ball with its bottom at the 1-metre mark. 2. Let go without pushing. 3. The other person watches the strip at eye level and calls out how high the bottom of the ball gets. 4. Do each ball 3 times.
flow.say: Just open your fingers. Don't throw it. Watch the strip. How high did it come back up?
flow.kid: Hold the ball at the top mark. Just let go. Watch how high it comes back. Try each ball 3 times.
flow.parent: The top of a bounce is fast, so it helps to do a test drop first and watch only the right part of the strip. A phone video in slow motion helps too.

flow.do: Drop the dough ball from 1 metre too.
flow.say: Now the dough. Does it bounce?
flow.kid: Drop the dough ball. Does it bounce? What shape is it now?

check.q: The dough ball did not bounce. It went flat. Why?
options: Dough is not elastic, so it does not spring back
It was dropped from too low
check.why: A bounce needs a squash and a spring back. Dough squashes but stays squashed. Picking 'too low' or 'too light' means looking for another cause. A rubber ball from the same height still bounces.

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart of the middle values.
flow.say: Let's draw one bar for each ball. A taller bar means a higher bounce.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each ball. Make it as tall as its middle bounce. Which ball is best?

chart.title: Made-up example results: how high each ball bounced back from 1 metre
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your balls will be different.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the rubber ball is the most elastic, so it bounces highest. What I saw: from 1 metre it bounced back 80 cm, but the dough ball did not bounce at all. Why: a ball bounces by squashing and springing back. Dough squashes but does not spring back. No ball comes all the way back, because some energy turns into heat and sound.

experiments.context: This is the Bounce Test. You drop different balls from 1 metre onto a hard floor and measure how high each one bounces back. A bounce is a squash and a spring back.

example_chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your balls will be different.

activities.title: Spring Hunt

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil, to list what you find

activities.safety: Go outdoors only with a grown-up. Only bend low, thin, living branches gently, and let them go slowly.

schedule.what: Hunt for springs and elastic things indoors, then on a short walk.

activities.record: Find 12 springs or elastic things. Write each one down. Next to it, write its job: to stretch, to squash, to bend or to bounce.

setup.art: A child opening a clothes peg and looking at its twisty spring.
setup.caption: 1. Hunt indoors: pens, pegs, beds, hair bands.

setup.art: A child gently bending a low green branch and watching it spring back.
setup.caption: 2. Outdoors: find a springy branch and bend it gently.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a list of springy things and little drawings beside each.
setup.caption: 3. Write each find and its job.

flow.do: Explain the hunt to your child, and give them the paper and pencil.
flow.say: We're spring detectives. Springs and elastic things are hiding all over our home. Let's find 12.
flow.kid: You are a spring detective! Find 12 springs or elastic things. Elastic means it springs back.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Spring Hunt. Elastic things change shape when pushed or pulled, and spring back when you let go.

flow.do: Hunt around the home, then outside. Look at pens, clothes pegs, the stapler, mattress and sofa, hair bands, pyjama elastic, a cycle seat, the spring balance at a shop, a charpai, and a low green branch.
flow.say: For each one, what is its job? Does it stretch, squash, bend or bounce? What would happen if it were not elastic?
flow.kid: For each find, say its job. Does it stretch, squash, bend or bounce? Write it down.
flow.parent: Good finds: the squash spring in a clicky pen, the twisty spring in a clothes peg, stretch springs in a spring balance or a trampoline, the elastic in socks, a hair band, the springs in a cycle seat. Outdoors, a low green branch bends and springs back. This tree-branch hunt is one of the founder's ideas.

flow.do: Ask each person to share their best find.
flow.say: Which find surprised you most? Which one would be a disaster if it were not elastic?
flow.kid: Which find surprised you most? Draw it.
flow.think: Who designed these springs? Why did they choose a spring, and not something stiff?

activities.context: This is a hunt around your home and street for springs and elastic things. You find out what job each one does.

activities.title: The Warm Rubber Band

materials.item: a thick, wide rubber band

activities.safety: Use a thick, wide band and stretch it only to about twice its length, so it cannot snap. Keep it away from your eyes.

schedule.what: Feel a rubber band warm up when stretched and cool when it springs back.

activities.record: Write down how the band felt on your forehead: before stretching, just after stretching, and just after letting it spring back.

setup.art: A child touching a thick rubber band to their forehead before stretching it.
setup.caption: 1. Touch the band to your forehead. Feel how warm it is.

setup.art: Two hands quickly stretching a thick rubber band, then pressing the stretched middle against the forehead.
setup.caption: 2. Stretch it fast. Touch it to your forehead again.

setup.art: The band relaxed again, touched to the forehead, with a little 'cool' symbol.
setup.caption: 3. Let it spring back slowly. Touch it again.

flow.do: Touch the middle of the thick rubber band to your forehead. Feel how warm it is.
flow.say: Feel the band on your forehead. Remember how warm it feels.
flow.kid: Touch the band to your forehead. How warm is it? Remember.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Warm Rubber Band. In 1805 a blind scientist, John Gough, found that rubber warms up when you stretch it. You can feel it too.

flow.do: 1. Hold the band near your forehead. 2. Stretch it quickly to about twice its length. 3. Straight away, touch the stretched middle to your forehead.
flow.say: Stretch it fast and touch it to your forehead straight away. What do you feel?
flow.kid: Stretch the band fast. Touch it to your forehead quickly. Warmer or cooler?

flow.do: 1. Keep it stretched for 10 seconds, away from your face. 2. Let it shrink back, still holding the ends. 3. Touch it to your forehead again.
flow.say: Now let it spring back and touch it again. What happened?
flow.kid: Keep it stretched for 10 seconds. Let it go back. Touch it again. Cooler?

check.q: A rubber band warms up when you stretch it fast. Why?
options: Its long tangled chains are pulled straight, and that makes heat
check.why: Stretching straightens rubber's tangled chains, and that gives out a little heat. Picking 'your fingers' is a fair guess, but your fingers only touch the ends. Picking 'the air rubs it' mixes this up with friction.

flow.do: Tell the story of John Gough.
flow.say: John Gough lived in Kendal, in England. He lost his sight to smallpox when he was a toddler. He still became a scientist, and he taught the famous chemist John Dalton. He held rubber against his lips, which feel heat very well. In 1805 he wrote about the warmth.
flow.kid: John Gough was blind. He was still a scientist. He felt rubber warm up on his lips. He wrote about it in 1805.
flow.think: John Gough could not see, but he found something everybody else missed. What can you notice without your eyes?

activities.context: In this activity you stretch a thick rubber band fast and feel it warm up on your forehead. A blind scientist called John Gough first noticed this in 1805.

activities.title: The Springs in My Body

materials.item: some open floor space and a soft mat

activities.safety: Jump on a soft mat or grass. Stop if anything hurts.

schedule.what: Feel your tendons, skin and pulse working like springs.

activities.record: Draw yourself jumping. Mark three springy parts of your body.

setup.art: A child jumping with stiff straight legs beside a child jumping with bent, bouncy legs.
setup.caption: 1. Jump with stiff legs, then with bendy legs.

setup.art: A child pinching the skin on the back of their hand and letting go.
setup.caption: 2. Pinch the skin on your hand. Let go.

setup.art: A child's fingers feeling the thick cord at the back of their ankle.
setup.caption: 3. Find your Achilles tendon at the back of your ankle.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to do 5 small jumps with stiff, straight knees. 2. Then 5 jumps with bendy, springy knees.
flow.say: Jump with stiff legs. Now jump with bendy legs. Which is easier? Which is higher?
flow.kid: Jump 5 times with stiff legs. Now 5 times with bendy knees. Which feels better?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Springs in My Body. Your body is full of parts that stretch and spring back, like springs.

flow.do: 1. Find the thick cord at the back of your ankle. 2. Stand on tiptoe and feel it go tight.
flow.say: This is your Achilles tendon. When you land from a jump, it stretches like a rubber band. When you push off, it springs back and helps you up.
flow.kid: Feel the back of your ankle. That cord is a tendon. Stand on tiptoe. Feel it go tight!

ask.q: Which animals use big springy tendons to hop?

flow.do: 1. Pinch the skin on the back of your hand and let go. Watch it. 2. Then press two fingers gently on the inside of your wrist and feel your pulse.
flow.say: Your skin springs back because of a stretchy stuff called elastin. That beat in your wrist is a blood vessel stretching each time your heart squeezes, then springing back.
flow.kid: Pinch your skin. Let go. It springs back! Now feel your wrist. That beat is a blood tube stretching.

check.q: Your skin springs back after a pinch. That means skin is…
check.why: Skin springs back, so it is elastic. Picking 'brittle' means skin was pictured snapping, which it does not. Picking 'stays changed' is what happens to dough, not skin.

flow.do: Tell your child about the flea.
flow.say: A flea jumps using a little pad of a rubbery stuff called resilin. It squashes the pad, locks it, then lets go all at once. It can jump many times its own height.
flow.kid: A flea has a tiny spring pad in its body. It squashes it, then lets go. Boing!
flow.think: If you were an animal designer, where would you put springs?

activities.context: In this activity you find the springs in your own body: your tendons, your skin and the blood vessel that beats in your wrist.

activities.title: Rubber Band Galaxies

materials.item: a wide rubber band, cut once to make a strip, or a strip of wide elastic
a felt pen and a ruler

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the band. Stretch it gently.

schedule.what: Draw galaxies on a band, stretch it and measure how they move apart.

activities.record: Write how far apart the dots were before and after stretching. Which dots moved apart the most?

setup.art: A wide rubber strip lying on a table with five dots drawn on it, 1 cm apart, labelled A to E.
setup.caption: 1. Draw 5 dots on the strip, 1 cm apart.

setup.art: Two hands stretching the strip to twice its length beside a ruler, the dots now 2 cm apart.
setup.caption: 2. Stretch it to twice as long.

setup.art: A ruler measuring from dot A to dot E on the stretched strip.
setup.caption: 3. Measure how far each dot moved from dot A.

flow.do: 1. Lay the strip flat. 2. Draw 5 dots, 1 cm apart. Label them A, B, C, D and E.
flow.say: Each dot is a galaxy, a giant family of stars. Dot A is our galaxy, the Milky Way.
flow.kid: Draw 5 dots, 1 cm apart. Each dot is a galaxy. Dot A is our home.
flow.context: This is the first step of Rubber Band Galaxies. The universe is slowly stretching. A rubber strip with dots on it shows how. This is one of the founder's ideas.

flow.do: 1. Stretch the strip to twice its length and hold it. 2. Measure from dot A to each other dot.
flow.say: Stretch it. Now how far is B from A? And E from A? Which dot moved further?
flow.kid: Stretch the strip to double. Measure from A to each dot. Which one moved furthest?

ask.q: Which dot moved away from A the most?

chart.title: Made-up example: how far each dot is from dot A

flow.do: Talk about the real universe.
flow.say: No dot is pushing the others. The rubber between them is stretching. Astronomers think space between galaxies is stretching in the same way. Far galaxies move away from us faster, just like dot E. And from any dot, all the others seem to move away. So there is no centre.
flow.kid: No dot moved by itself. The rubber stretched. Space between galaxies stretches too. Far ones move away faster!

check.q: On the stretched strip, which dot moved furthest from dot A?
check.why: The furthest dot moved most, because there is more stretching rubber between it and dot A. Picking 'nearest' or 'all the same' means the dots were pictured moving by themselves. It is the rubber between them that stretches.

flow.think: If you lived on dot C, would you think you were at the centre? Is anyone at the centre?

activities.context: In this activity you draw dots on a rubber strip and stretch it. It shows how the universe is stretching, with galaxies getting further apart.

activities.title: Rubber Band Orchestra

materials.item: an empty tissue box or an open shoe box
4 rubber bands of different thicknesses
2 pencils

activities.safety: Pluck gently. Keep faces away from tight bands.

schedule.what: Make a rubber band box guitar and test how stretch and thickness change the note.

activities.record: Write which band makes the highest note and which makes the lowest. Write what happens when you stretch a band tighter.

setup.art: An open shoe box with four rubber bands of different thicknesses stretched round it, two pencils under the bands as bridges.
setup.caption: 1. Stretch 4 bands round a box. Slide 2 pencils under them.

setup.art: A finger plucking one rubber band, which blurs as it vibrates.
setup.caption: 2. Pluck each band. Listen.

setup.art: A hand pulling one band tighter round the box while another hand plucks it.
setup.caption: 3. Stretch one band tighter. Pluck again.

flow.do: 1. Stretch the four bands round the box, over the opening. 2. Slide a pencil under the bands at each end.
flow.say: Let's build a guitar from springs. Each band is a spring that we will pluck.
flow.kid: Put 4 bands round the box. Slide a pencil under them at each end. Now you have a guitar!
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rubber Band Orchestra, one of the founder's ideas. A plucked rubber band springs back and forth very fast. That makes a sound.

flow.do: 1. Pluck each band and listen. 2. Watch how it blurs.
flow.say: When you pluck it, it springs back, overshoots, and springs back again, very fast. That shaking is called vibrating. It makes the note.
flow.kid: Pluck each band. Watch it blur. It is springing back and forth very fast!

ask.q: Which band makes the lowest note?

flow.do: Pull one band tighter round the box, and pluck it again.
flow.say: The tighter it's stretched, the harder it pulls back, so the faster it shakes. Faster shaking makes a higher note.
flow.kid: Stretch one band tighter. Pluck it. Higher note or lower?

check.q: You stretch a rubber band tighter and pluck it. What happens to the note?
check.why: A tighter band pulls back harder and shakes faster, which makes a higher note. Picking 'lower' often comes from thinking a longer stretch must sound deeper. Listen again to check.

flow.do: Talk about Indian instruments and C. V. Raman.
flow.say: A veena, a sitar and a tabla all use stretched strings or stretched skins. In 1920, the Indian scientist C. V. Raman worked out why Indian drums like the tabla and mridangam sound so musical.
flow.kid: A veena and a tabla use stretched strings and skins. C. V. Raman, an Indian scientist, studied why they sound so sweet.
flow.think: Which instruments in your home or temple use something stretched?

activities.context: In this activity you build a box guitar from rubber bands. You find out how stretching a band tighter changes its note.

activities.title: Bend or Snap? Twigs and the Ruler Earthquake

materials.item: a fresh green twig and a dry dead twig of about the same thickness
a plastic ruler

activities.safety: Snap twigs pointing away from faces. Do not bend the ruler until it breaks. Pick twigs that have already fallen, or ask before taking a small piece.

schedule.what: Bend a green and a dry twig. Make a ruler 'earthquake'.

activities.record: Draw the green twig and the dry twig after bending. Write which one sprang back.

setup.art: Two hands bending a green twig into a curve, and beside it a dry twig snapping.
setup.caption: 1. Bend a green twig and a dry twig.

setup.art: A plastic ruler held flat on a table with one end hanging over the edge, a finger pressing the end down.
setup.caption: 2. Hold a ruler on the table. Press the free end down slowly.

setup.art: The ruler end slipping off the finger and springing up with a twang, shaking lines around it.
setup.caption: 3. Let your finger slip off. Twang! That is an earthquake.

flow.do: 1. Gently bend the green twig, then let go. 2. Gently bend the dry twig the same amount.
flow.say: Which one bends and comes back? Which one snaps? Why do you think the living one is springier?
flow.kid: Bend the green twig. Let go. Now bend the dry twig. Which one snapped?
flow.context: This is the first step of Bend or Snap?. You compare a living twig and a dead one. Then you use a ruler to show how earthquakes happen.

flow.do: 1. Hold a plastic ruler flat on a table with about half of it over the edge. 2. Press the free end down slowly with one finger. 3. Keep pressing until it slips off your finger.
flow.say: Rock underground gets bent slowly, like this ruler, for years and years. Then it slips. Feel what happens when it slips.
flow.kid: Hold the ruler on the table. Press the end down slowly. Keep going until it slips. Twang!

ask.q: What happened when the ruler slipped?
good: It made a twang and wobbled.

flow.parent: The ruler stores energy as it bends. When it slips, the energy is let go all at once, as shaking and sound. Underground rock does the same, and the shaking is an earthquake.

flow.do: Bend the green twig again, a little more each time. Each time, check if it springs all the way back.
flow.say: In the story, Ammu saw that the swing branch stopped coming all the way back. Let's watch for that sign on our green twig.
flow.kid: Bend the green twig a bit more each time. Does it still come all the way back?

check.q: A branch bends under a swing. When you get off, it stays a little bent. What does that warn you?
options: It has passed its elastic limit and may break soon
It is fine, because it is still bending
check.why: A branch that stays bent has passed its elastic limit, so it may break soon. Picking 'it is fine' is a common idea, because bending itself is safe. The warning is when it stops coming back. Picking 'stronger' is the opposite of what happens.

flow.think: Is bending a kind of strength?

activities.context: In this activity you bend a green twig and a dry twig to see which springs back. You bend a ruler until it slips, to feel how an earthquake happens. Then you watch a twig for the warning sign of the elastic limit.

projects.title: The Rubber Band Car

materials.item: a small empty plastic bottle or a juice carton
4 bottle caps for wheels
2 wooden skewers or thin sticks for axles, and 2 drinking straws
2 or 3 rubber bands
tape, and a paper clip
a measuring tape or a long strip of paper marked every 10 cm

projects.safety: A grown-up makes all holes in the caps and the bottle, using a hot skewer or a sharp tool. Snip the sharp tips off skewers.

schedule.what: Build the car body and the wheels.
Add the rubber band motor. Test it with 5, 10 and 15 winds.
Improve the car and hold a race.

projects.record: Write how far the car went with 5, 10 and 15 winds. Draw your car and label where the energy is stored.

setup.art: A plastic bottle lying on its side with two straws taped across its underside, a skewer through each straw, and bottle caps pushed on the ends as wheels.
setup.caption: 1. Tape two straws under the bottle. Push skewers through. Add cap wheels.

setup.art: A rubber band hooked to a paper clip at the front of the bottle, its other end looped round the back axle.
setup.caption: 2. Hook a rubber band from the front to the back axle.

setup.art: A child turning the back wheels backwards so the band winds round the axle.
setup.caption: 3. Wind the back wheels backwards. The band twists round the axle.

setup.art: The car rolling along the floor beside a paper strip marked every 10 cm.
setup.caption: 4. Let go and measure how far it goes.

flow.do: 1. Tape two straws across the bottom of the bottle, one near each end. 2. Push a skewer through each straw. 3. A grown-up makes a hole in the middle of each cap. 4. Push a cap onto each end of each skewer.
flow.say: We're building a car that runs on a rubber band. First, the body and the wheels.
flow.kid: Tape two straws under the bottle. Push a stick through each one. A grown-up makes holes in the caps. Push on the wheels.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rubber Band Car project. You build a little car whose motor is a twisted rubber band.

flow.do: 1. Check that the wheels turn freely. 2. If they rub on the bottle, slide the straws further out. 3. Roll the car gently to test it.
flow.say: A good car rolls easily. If a wheel rubs, friction steals the energy. Let's fix it.
flow.kid: Spin each wheel. Does it turn easily? If it rubs, move the straw. Roll the car.
flow.parent: Wheels that wobble or rub are the most common problem. A drop of oil or soap on the skewer can help.

flow.do: 1. Hook one end of a rubber band on a paper clip taped to the front of the bottle. 2. Loop the other end round the back axle and tape it once to the axle.
flow.say: Now the motor. When we wind the wheels, the band twists round the axle and stores energy.
flow.kid: Hook a band to the front. Loop it round the back axle. Tape it on. That is the motor!
flow.wait: Leave the car for the next day's tests.

flow.do: 1. Turn the back wheels backwards 5 times. 2. Put the car down at the start of the paper strip and let go. 3. Measure how far it goes. 4. Repeat with 10 winds and 15 winds.
flow.say: Five winds. Let go! How far? Now ten. What do you think will happen?
flow.kid: Wind the back wheels backwards 5 times. Let go. Measure. Now try 10 winds, then 15.

check.q: The car went further with 15 winds than with 5 winds. Why?
options: The band stored more energy when wound more
check.why: More winds twist the band more, so it stores more energy. Picking 'lighter' or 'smoother floor' means looking for another cause. Only the winds changed.

chart.title: Made-up example: how far the rubber band car went
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your car will be different.

flow.do: 1. Choose one thing to improve: a second band, bigger wheels, or less rubbing. 2. Change only that one thing and test again.
flow.say: Engineers change one thing at a time. Then they know what made the difference. What will you change?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Maybe two bands, or bigger wheels. Test it again. Better or worse?
flow.parent: Too many winds can snap the band or make the wheels spin and skid. That is the elastic limit again.

flow.do: Hold a race with family or friends. Ask your child to explain how the car works.
flow.say: Tell everyone where the energy comes from, and where it is stored.
flow.kid: Race your car! Then explain it. Where is the energy stored?
flow.think: Your arm wound the band. Where did your arm get the energy from?

projects.context: In this 3-day project, you build a little car from a bottle and bottle caps. Its motor is a rubber band that you twist round the back axle. The twisted band stores energy and turns the wheels.

challenges.title: The Catapult Challenge
challenges.problem: Build a catapult from ice-cream sticks and rubber bands. It must land a paper ball in a bowl 1 metre away.
constraints: Use only ice-cream sticks, rubber bands, a plastic spoon or bottle cap, and tape.
Never aim at people, animals or windows.
materials: a plastic spoon or bottle cap
general: Stack 6 sticks and tie them with bands at both ends. Put this stack between 2 more sticks tied together at one end. The top stick becomes the arm.
Tape a bottle cap or spoon to the end of the arm to hold the paper ball.
Pull the arm down further to fire further. More bend stores more energy.
creative: Change the stack height. A taller stack lets the arm bend further.
Use two rubber bands at the front to make a stiffer spring.
Mark lines on the arm and test how far each pull-back fires. Then you can aim like a scientist, not by guessing.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own design. Draw it, build it, and test it. Can you hit the bowl 3 times in a row?

setup.art: A stack of six ice-cream sticks tied with rubber bands at both ends.
setup.caption: 1. Tie a stack of 6 sticks.

setup.art: Two sticks tied together at one end, with the stack pushed between them, making a V shape.
setup.caption: 2. Push the stack between two sticks tied at one end.

setup.art: A bottle cap taped to the top stick, a paper ball in it, a finger pressing the arm down.
setup.caption: 3. Tape on a cap. Load a paper ball. Press down and let go.

setup.art: A bowl on the floor 1 metre away with a paper ball flying towards it.
setup.caption: 4. Aim for the bowl 1 metre away.

flow.do: Build the basic catapult with your child, using the usual design.
flow.say: The arm is a bent stick. When we press it down, it stores energy. When we let go, it springs back.
flow.kid: Build the catapult. Tie the stack. Push it between two sticks. Tape on the cap.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Catapult Challenge. You build a catapult from ice-cream sticks and rubber bands, and aim at a bowl. Building a catapult is one of the founder's ideas.
flow.parent: Building it is the slowest part. If the bands keep slipping, wrap them twice.

flow.do: 1. Press the arm down a little and fire. 2. Then press it down a lot. 3. Measure how far each one goes.
flow.say: Small press, big press. What changes?
flow.kid: Press the arm down a little. Fire. Now press a lot. Fire. Measure both.

check.q: Pressing the catapult arm down further makes the paper ball go…
options: Further, because more energy is stored
Less far, because the arm gets tired
check.why: Pressing further bends the arm more and stores more energy. Picking 'the arm gets tired' pictures the stick like a tired person. Sticks do not tire like that, though bending it too far could snap it.

flow.do: Mark lines on the arm. Fire from each line and measure. Then use your marks to aim for the bowl.
flow.say: Scientists don't guess. They measure. Which line gets the ball to 1 metre?
flow.kid: Mark lines on the arm. Fire from each one. Which line reaches the bowl?

flow.do: Read the usual and the creative ideas together, then invent something new.
flow.say: People have used bent wood and twisted ropes to throw things for thousands of years. What can you invent?
flow.kid: Look at the ideas. Now invent your own change. Can you hit the bowl 3 times?
flow.think: A bow, a catapult and a trampoline all store energy by bending. What else does?

challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You build a catapult from ice-cream sticks and rubber bands. You aim a paper ball into a bowl 1 metre away.

challenges.title: Bungee Doll
challenges.problem: A small doll or soft toy goes on a 'bungee jump' from a table. It hangs from a chain of rubber bands. Make it fall as close to the floor as you can, without its head touching.
constraints: Use only rubber bands, all the same size.
You must predict how many bands to use before the final jump.
The doll must not touch the floor.
materials: a small doll or soft toy
15 to 20 rubber bands of the same size
general: Test with 2, 3 and 4 bands. Measure how far the doll falls each time.
Find how much further each extra band lets it fall.
Measure the table height and work out how many bands fit.
creative: Draw a line graph of bands and fall distance. Use the line to predict.
Use a thicker band at the top to make the chain stiffer.
Real bungee cords are bundles of many thin rubber strands, which work like many bands side by side.
challenges.your_turn: Now make your prediction. How many bands? Test it once. How close did you get?

setup.art: A chain of rubber bands looped together, one through the next.
setup.caption: 1. Loop rubber bands into a chain.

setup.art: A doll tied by its feet to the end of a short chain of bands, the other end held at a table edge.
setup.caption: 2. Tie the doll's feet to the chain. Hold the top at the table edge.

setup.art: The doll dropping down below the table, the chain stretched, with a ruler standing on the floor beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Drop the doll. Measure how far down it gets.

setup.art: The doll hanging just above the floor at the lowest point of its jump.
setup.caption: 4. Predict the number of bands for the closest safe jump.

flow.do: 1. Make a chain of 2 rubber bands. 2. Tie it round the doll's feet. 3. Hold the top end at the table edge, with the doll at the edge too.
flow.say: This doll is going bungee jumping. We'll find out how many bands she needs to come close to the floor, but not touch it.
flow.kid: Loop 2 bands together. Tie them to the doll's feet. Hold the top at the table edge.
flow.context: This is the first step of Bungee Doll. A doll hangs from a chain of rubber bands and drops off a table. You must predict how many bands to use.

flow.do: 1. Drop the doll and watch its lowest point. 2. Measure from the table top to the doll's head at its lowest point. 3. Repeat with 3 and 4 bands. 4. Write the results in a table.
flow.say: Watch the lowest point, not where it ends up. How much further did each extra band let it fall?
flow.kid: Drop the doll. Watch its lowest point. Measure it. Now try 3 bands, then 4. Write them down.
flow.parent: A phone video helps you see the lowest point. Each extra band usually adds about the same extra distance.

chart.title: Made-up example: how far the doll fell
cols: Lowest point below the table top (cm)

flow.do: 1. Measure the table height. 2. Work out how many bands should bring the doll close to the floor. 3. Make your prediction and test it.
flow.say: Each band added 10 cm. The table is 75 cm tall. How many bands would bring the doll to about 70 cm?
flow.kid: Measure the table. Each band adds about 10 cm. How many bands do you need? Test it!

check.q: 2 bands: 30 cm. 3 bands: 40 cm. 4 bands: 50 cm. How far for 6 bands?
check.why: Each extra band adds 10 cm. 4 bands is 50 cm, so 6 bands is 2 more bands: 50 + 20 = 70 cm. Picking 60 cm usually means counting 10 cm for each band from zero. Picking 100 cm doubles 50, but the pattern adds, it does not double.

flow.do: Compare your prediction with what happened, then read the ideas together.
flow.say: How close did you get? What would you change?
flow.kid: How close did you get? What would you change next time?
flow.think: Real bungee jumpers trust their lives to this kind of maths. Why must engineers test cords many times?

challenges.context: This is a prediction challenge. A doll on a chain of rubber bands drops from a table. You test, find the pattern, and predict how many bands to use so it gets close to the floor without touching.

videos.title: Slinky drop in slow motion
videos.why: Shows a stretched spring in slow motion. The bottom of a dropped Slinky stays still in the air until the top crashes into it. It shows that a spring takes time to spring back.
videos.check: Found by YouTube search: "Supersized Slow-Mo Slinky Drop" by Veritasium. Title checked automatically; a parent may still preview it.

videos.title: LIGO's first gravitational wave, as sound
videos.why: Plays the 'chirp' of the first gravitational wave, caught in 2015, turned into sound. It helps children feel that space itself was stretched and squeezed.
videos.check: Found by YouTube search: "Direct Detection of Gravitational Waves: What Does That Mean?" by LIGO Lab Caltech : MIT. Title checked automatically; a parent may still preview it.

videos.title: Tapping a rubber tree for latex
videos.channel: to choose: the Rubber Board of India or a reliable broadcaster
videos.why: Shows the real work from the story: tapping rubber trees, collecting latex, rolling it into sheets and smoking them. (Filmed in Thailand; tapping in Kerala works the same way.)
