opts: It springs back to its shape when you let go
quiz.why: Elastic things change shape and then spring back. Picking 'soft' is common, but a steel spring is hard and elastic.
A sponge springs back. Playdough stays changed. A dry twig snaps. Picking playdough often means changing shape was mixed up with springing back.

quiz.p: In the coin stretch test, what should you change to make it a fair test?
quiz.why: Change only one thing at a time. Then you know what caused the change. Picking 'coins and cup' means testing two things at once.
quiz.context: In the coin stretch test, you hang a paper cup from a rubber band and add coins, 5 at a time.

quiz.p: Look at the line graph. With 0 coins the band was 10 cm, and each 5 coins added 1 cm. How long was it with 25 coins?
quiz.why: 25 coins is 5 lots of 5 coins. That adds 5 cm. 10 + 5 = 15 cm. Picking 25 cm means the coins were read as centimetres.

chart.title: Made-up example: length of a rubber band as coins are added
chart.note: Each 5 coins made the band about 1 cm longer. The line is straight.

quiz.p: A spring is pulled far past its elastic limit. When you let go, what happens?
opts: It stays stretched, or it snaps
quiz.why: Past the limit, a spring cannot get back. Picking 'perfectly' means elastic was thought to have no limit.

quiz.p: Which of these snaps rather than bending or stretching?
quiz.why: A papad is brittle. It hardly bends before it snaps. Picking chewing gum mixes up stays-changed with snapping.

quiz.p: Why does a stretched catapult fling a paper ball?
opts: The stretched band stores energy and gives it back
quiz.why: Stretching stores energy. Letting go turns it into movement. Picking 'the ball is light' is true but is not what flings it.

quiz.p: A ball bounces. What happens when it hits the floor?
opts: It squashes for a moment, then springs back
quiz.why: A bounce is a squash and a spring back. Picking 'stays round' is natural, because the squash is too fast to see.

quiz.p: Which spring is in a clicky pen?
opts: A squash spring that pushes the tip back in
quiz.why: Pressing the pen squashes its spring. It pushes the tip back in when you click again.

quiz.p: Which part of your body works like a spring when you run?
quiz.why: The tendon at the back of your ankle stretches as you land and springs back as you push off.

quiz.p: Deep down, why do solid things spring back?
opts: Atoms are held by electric pulls that act like tiny springs
quiz.why: Bonds between atoms act like tiny springs. Picking gravity misses that springs work in every direction.

quiz.p: Why does a rubber band warm up when you stretch it fast?
opts: Its tangled chains are pulled straight, and that gives out heat
quiz.why: This is rubber's special secret, found by John Gough in 1805. Picking 'your hand' is a fair guess, but it warms even if you only hold the ends.

opts: Bent rock underground suddenly slips and springs back
quiz.why: Rock bends slowly for years, then slips. Picking 'buildings sink' mixes up the cause with the damage.

quiz.p: What does a gravitational wave do?
opts: It stretches and squeezes space itself, by a tiny amount
It is a wave of light
quiz.why: Gravitational waves are ripples in space. Picking 'the sea' mixes them up with tides or ocean waves.

quiz.p: Do scientists know what space is made of?
opts: No, it is still an open question
Yes, it is made of rubber
Yes, it is made of air
quiz.why: We can measure space stretching, but not what it is made of. Picking 'rubber' takes the rubber-sheet picture too literally.

applications: Spring balances at vegetable shops, luggage scales and forcemeters measure weight by how far a spring stretches.
Clicky pens, staplers, clothes pegs, door latches and mousetraps use small springs.
Mattresses, sofas, cycle seats and charpais are springy so they are comfortable.
Cars, buses, autos and trains have big springs and shock absorbers to soften bumps.
Wind-up watches and clocks run on a coiled spring. HMT made wind-up watches in Bengaluru for decades.
Catapults, bows and slingshots store energy in stretched wood and rubber.
Rubber bands, hair bands and the elastic in clothes hold things snugly.
Balls for cricket, football and tennis are tested for how well they bounce.
Trampolines and diving boards bend and spring back to throw people up.
Bungee cords are bundles of rubber strands that stretch to stop a fall gently.
Musical instruments like the veena, sitar, violin and tabla use stretched strings and skins.
Earthquake-safe buildings are designed to sway and spring back instead of cracking.
Doctors use springy wires to straighten teeth and springy stents to hold blood vessels open.
Scientists copy spider silk and resilin to try to make new, tougher materials.
LIGO and the future LIGO-India use the stretching of space to listen to black holes crashing far away.

open_questions.q: What is space made of, that it can stretch and ripple?
open_questions.why_open: We can measure space stretching, but nobody knows what it is made of. String theory and loop quantum gravity are ideas, with no evidence yet.

open_questions.q: Exactly how do spiders make silk that is so strong and so stretchy, and can we make it in factories?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know a lot about the proteins in silk. But copying how the spider spins it, at a large scale, is still very hard.

open_questions.q: Can we predict when bent rock will slip and cause an earthquake?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can measure rock slowly bending. But they still cannot say when it will slip.

open_questions.q: Why do springs and rubber get 'tired' and crack after being stretched many times?
open_questions.why_open: This is called fatigue. Engineers test it carefully, but exactly when a crack will start is still hard to predict.

open_questions.q: How exactly does titin, the giant spring protein in our muscles, work?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know titin acts like a spring, but how all its parts work together is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Can we always see the warning signs before something breaks?
open_questions.why_open: A thing that stays bent is a warning. But tiny cracks can grow inside without showing. Engineers use sound waves and X-rays to look, and still cannot catch everything.

open_questions.q: Could there be a perfectly elastic material that gives back all of its energy?
open_questions.why_open: Every real material turns a little energy into heat each time it springs back. Resilin comes close. Nobody knows how close anything can get.

ask_kids: You just sat on the sofa. Did it spring back when you stood up?
Which is elastic: the roti dough or the rubber band holding the bag? How do you know?
Why does the spring balance at the shop move further with a heavier bag?
That ball bounced. Where did it squash?
Can you find a spring in this room?
When you jump, which parts of your legs are springs?
What would happen if hair bands were not elastic?
That tree is bending in the wind. Why doesn't it snap?
Is anything completely stiff? Does the floor bend when you stand on it?
Have you ever felt stretched too far, like a rubber band? What helped you spring back?
Space can stretch. What do you think space is made of?

jokes.j: Why did the rubber band go to school?
jokes.a: It wanted to stretch its mind.

jokes.j: What season do springs like best?

maths.problem: In the coin stretch test, the thin band was 10 cm long with no coins. Each 5 coins made it 1 cm longer. How long will it be with 30 coins? Use the line graph to help.
maths.explain: 30 coins is 6 lots of 5 coins, because 30 divided by 5 is 6. Each lot adds 1 cm, so the band grows 6 cm. 10 + 6 = 16 cm. On the graph, the line keeps going up 1 cm for every 5 coins.
maths.why_maths: A line graph lets you see the pattern in your stretch results and predict a result you have not measured yet.
maths.context: In the coin stretch test, you hang a paper cup from a rubber band and add coins, 5 at a time. You measure the band each time.

maths.problem: Look at the ruler beside the rubber band in the picture. The big numbers are centimetres. Each small mark is half a centimetre. The bottom of the band is at the small mark just after 12. How long is the band?
maths.explain: The bottom of the band is past 12 but before 13. It is on the small mark halfway between them. Each small mark is half a centimetre. So the band is 12 and a half centimetres long.
maths.why_maths: Each 5 coins stretch the band only a little, so you need to read half centimetres to see the change.

maths.problem: In the Bungee Doll challenge, 2 bands let the doll fall 30 cm, 3 bands 40 cm and 4 bands 50 cm. The table is 75 cm tall. What is the most bands you can use so the doll's lowest point stays above the floor?
maths.answer: 6 bands. The doll falls 70 cm, which is 5 cm above the floor. 7 bands would be 80 cm, which hits the floor.
maths.explain: Each extra band adds 10 cm. 5 bands make 60 cm. 6 bands make 70 cm. 7 bands make 80 cm. The table is 75 cm tall. 70 cm is less than 75 cm, so 6 bands is safe. 80 cm is more than 75 cm, so 7 bands would hit the floor.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the number pattern in your bungee tests lets you predict a safe jump before you try it.
maths.context: In the Bungee Doll challenge, a doll on a chain of rubber bands drops off a table. You measure how far down it gets.

maths.problem: In the Bounce Test, these balls were dropped from 100 cm. Rubber ball 80 cm, tennis ball 55 cm, sponge ball 20 cm, plastic ball 40 cm. Draw a bar chart. Then answer: how much higher did the rubber ball bounce than the sponge ball?
maths.answer: 60 cm higher. Here is the bar chart.
maths.explain: Draw one bar for each ball, as tall as its bounce. The rubber ball bounced 80 cm. The sponge ball bounced 20 cm. 80 take away 20 is 60. So the rubber ball bounced 60 cm higher.
maths.why_maths: After the bounce test you have a list of heights. A bar chart shows the most elastic ball at a glance.
maths.context: In the Bounce Test, you drop different balls from 1 metre and measure how high each one bounces back.

maths.problem: Your rubber band car went 60 cm with 5 winds. Suppose every 5 winds add about the same distance. About how far would it go with 15 winds? Then compare with the real result of 180 cm.
maths.answer: About 180 cm. That matches the real result.
maths.explain: 15 winds is 3 lots of 5 winds. Each lot gives about 60 cm. 3 × 60 = 180 cm. The real car went 180 cm, so the guess was right. With many more winds, the band would reach its limit, and the pattern would stop working.
maths.why_maths: Thinking in equal groups of winds helps you predict how far the car will go before you test it.
